title: Accountants and auditors
rationale: Accounting and auditing are heavily digital, rules-based, document-centered, and analytical, making many tasks such as transaction coding, reconciliations, tax preparation, audit sampling, anomaly detection, and report drafting highly exposed to AI and automation. However, the occupation still requires professional judgment, regulatory accountability, client communication, audit signoff, and interpretation of ambiguous business situations, so AI is more likely to transform workflows than eliminate the role outright. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper accounting can unlock more advisory services, better controls, and higher-quality analysis for small businesses and individuals, but many core needs such as annual audits, tax filings, and compliance cycles are structurally limited. This fits a restructure outcome: routine production work shrinks while accountants who can supervise AI, validate outputs, manage risk, and provide strategic advice remain valuable.

title: Actors
rationale: Acting has an embodied, interpersonal, and live-performance component that AI cannot fully replicate, especially in theater, theme parks, and high-status screen roles. However, a large share of recorded-media work—voiceover, dubbing, extras, commercials, background performances, synthetic avatars, and some low-budget screen acting—is directly exposed to generative audio and video tools, making disruption high. Demand could expand as cheaper production enables more ads, games, training videos, localization, and niche entertainment, but audience attention, celebrity economics, union rules, and preference for human performers limit how much of that expansion becomes employment for actors. The occupation is therefore likely to be substantially restructured, with more value placed on distinctive human performance, likeness rights, live work, and hybrid AI-production skills.

title: Actuaries
rationale: Actuarial work is highly digital and analytical: compiling data, building statistical models, pricing products, calculating reserves, writing reports, and explaining results are all tasks that AI can substantially accelerate. Human actuaries will still be needed for regulatory accountability, professional judgment, assumptions governance, and communication with executives and regulators, but much of the junior and mid-level modeling, coding, documentation, and scenario analysis is directly exposed. Demand for actuarial analysis may expand somewhat as firms model more risks, personalize insurance products, and use enterprise risk management more broadly, but insurance regulation, required sign-offs, and the limited number of pricing/reserving decisions constrain expansion. Because disruption is high and elasticity is relatively low, productivity gains are likely to reduce the number of actuaries needed for many routine analytical functions, even if senior credentialed roles remain important.

title: Administrative services and facilities managers
rationale: AI will materially change the administrative, records, compliance, procurement, scheduling, reporting, and energy-analysis portions of this occupation, and AI-enabled building systems can support predictive maintenance and monitoring. However, much of facilities management still requires onsite judgment, vendor coordination, staff supervision, emergency response, inspections, and accountability for safety and regulatory compliance in physical spaces. Demand elasticity is limited because organizations do not need dramatically more facilities management simply because it becomes cheaper; demand is tied to the number, size, and complexity of buildings and organizations. Because disruption is significant but not high enough to fully reshape the physical and managerial core of the job, the occupation fits the resilient category.

title: Adult basic and secondary education and ESL teachers
rationale: Much of this occupation is language-based and cognitive: lesson planning, explaining concepts, grading, progress monitoring, individualized practice, and ESL conversation support are all areas where AI tutors and adaptive learning tools are already useful. However, teachers still provide motivation, classroom management, cultural sensitivity, assessment of nonacademic barriers, and connections to community resources, which keeps disruption below the most automatable digital occupations. Demand could expand because cheaper personalized instruction would help adults who cannot attend scheduled classes or afford tutoring, especially ESL learners, but growth is limited by public funding, student time constraints, credentialing needs, and declining adult education enrollment. The result is a substantial shift in the teacher role toward facilitation, coaching, assessment, and support rather than straightforward replacement, so the net effect is restructure.

title: Advertising sales agents
rationale: Advertising sales agents perform highly language- and information-based work: prospecting, writing outreach, preparing pitches, generating proposals, recommending ad formats, maintaining CRM records, and analyzing account performance. AI and automated ad platforms can already handle much of lead generation, campaign recommendation, proposal drafting, reporting, and self-service ad placement, although human relationship-building and complex negotiations remain important for larger accounts. Demand for advertising is not fixed, but it is constrained by client budgets, available attention, and measurable ROI; cheaper sales support may help small advertisers somewhat but will not create proportionate demand for human agents. Because disruption is high and elasticity is relatively low, AI is likely to reduce headcount while leaving a smaller group focused on strategic relationship management and complex accounts.

title: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers
rationale: This occupation is heavily cognitive, digital, and language-based: market research, campaign planning, audience segmentation, pricing analysis, copy and creative evaluation, media optimization, and reporting are all areas where AI tools are already materially useful. However, the role also includes client relationships, cross-functional coordination, negotiation, budget accountability, brand judgment, and staff management, which keep it from being fully automatable. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper marketing enables more personalization, experimentation, and access for smaller firms, but total demand is limited by consumer attention, firm budgets, and the need for accountable human decision-makers. The best fit is restructure: AI will substantially change workflows and reduce demand for some routine campaign and analysis tasks, while increasing the value of managers who can use AI strategically and oversee more complex marketing systems.

title: Aerospace engineering and operations technologists and technicians
rationale: AI will materially affect the analytical and digital parts of this job, including test-data analysis, simulation setup, calibration diagnostics, documentation, and troubleshooting recommendations. However, the core work still involves physical test facilities, instrumentation, aircraft or spacecraft hardware, safety procedures, and hands-on installation and maintenance that require human presence in controlled environments. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper testing and analysis could support more satellite, drone, electric aircraft, and aerospace R&D projects, but growth is limited by capital intensity, regulation, safety certification, and physical testing bottlenecks. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to displace the hands-on core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Aerospace engineers
rationale: Aerospace engineering is heavily computer-based and cognitive, involving modeling, simulation, requirements analysis, design review, documentation, and troubleshooting, all of which AI can significantly accelerate. However, the work remains tied to physical systems, safety certification, testing, manufacturing constraints, and multidisciplinary accountability, so AI is unlikely to fully absorb the occupation. Demand would expand as cheaper engineering enables more satellite, drone, defense, propulsion, and aircraft redesign projects, but growth is limited by capital costs, regulation, testing cycles, and procurement bottlenecks. This fits a restructure outcome: core workflows and skill requirements change substantially, but demand and real-world constraints prevent simple replacement.

title: Agricultural and food science technicians
rationale: This occupation combines hands-on sample collection, lab preparation, equipment operation, field or plant work, and sterile/safety procedures with cognitive tasks such as recording results, analyzing data, and writing reports. AI can meaningfully improve the analytical and documentation portions, including anomaly detection, image-based disease identification, experiment tracking, and report generation, but much of the core work still requires physical presence in labs, farms, processing plants, and greenhouses. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper testing and analysis could lead to more frequent food safety checks, soil testing, crop monitoring, and agricultural R&D, especially under climate and supply-chain pressures, though regulation, budgets, and physical sampling needs limit unlimited expansion. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment workflows and change tools than to fundamentally replace the occupation.

title: Agricultural and food scientists
rationale: Agricultural and food scientists do substantial knowledge work—literature review, experimental design, statistical analysis, modeling, technical writing, regulatory documentation, and product or breeding optimization—that AI can materially accelerate. However, much of the occupation still depends on laboratory experiments, field trials, biological growth cycles, food-processing constraints, inspections, and hands-on implementation, so AI is unlikely to fully automate the role. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper research could expand work on climate resilience, food safety, crop productivity, sustainable inputs, and new food products, but demand is constrained by regulation, validation requirements, capital equipment, and biological timelines. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is best categorized as restructure: scientists will remain needed, but workflows and required skills will shift strongly toward AI-enabled data science, automation, and model-guided experimentation.

title: Agricultural engineers
rationale: Agricultural engineers do substantial cognitive and digital work—CAD design, modeling, simulation, data analysis, and increasingly AI/geospatial integration—so AI will meaningfully change workflows and raise productivity. However, the occupation remains tied to physical equipment, farms, facilities, environmental conditions, testing, construction oversight, safety, and licensed engineering judgment, which limits full automation of the core role. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper engineering could accelerate precision agriculture, automation, irrigation, biofuels, and environmental compliance projects, but adoption is constrained by farm capital budgets, regulation, and the physical pace of implementation. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to fully reshape or replace the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Agricultural workers
rationale: Most agricultural worker tasks are physical, outdoor, and variable—planting, harvesting, feeding, herding, cleaning, repairing, and handling animals or crops—so current AI alone cannot perform the core job without substantial robotics and machinery. AI-enabled precision agriculture, autonomous tractors, robotic harvesters, sensors, and advanced irrigation will change some workflows and reduce some manual labor, especially in large-scale crop production, but adoption will be uneven across crops, farms, and regions. Demand elasticity is low because food demand is constrained by population, diets, land, water, and biological growing cycles, so cheaper labor does not lead consumers to buy many times more agricultural output. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate rather than primarily digital or AI-substitutable, the occupation fits the resilient category despite gradual mechanization-driven employment pressure.

title: Air traffic controllers
rationale: Air traffic control is highly cognitive, real-time, and screen/radio-mediated, with core tasks such as monitoring aircraft, detecting conflicts, sequencing traffic, and issuing clearances all in the path of advanced automation and AI decision-support systems. However, safety certification, liability, and the need for human oversight in abnormal situations will slow full substitution, so the disruption score is high but not maximal. Demand elasticity is low because the number of controllers needed is tied mainly to flight volumes, airport capacity, and regulation; cheaper controller labor would not cause society to fly several times more. Given high disruption and low elasticity, AI-enabled productivity would mostly reduce staffing needs over time rather than unlock enough new demand to offset displacement.

title: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians
rationale: AI can materially assist the diagnostic and documentation portions of this occupation, including troubleshooting avionics faults, interpreting maintenance manuals, analyzing sensor data, and generating records. However, the core work remains hands-on, safety-critical, site-specific repair, inspection, installation, and testing of physical aircraft systems under FAA certification requirements, so AI is unlikely to absorb most daily tasks within 10 years. Demand is only modestly elastic because maintenance is tied to fleet size, flight activity, and regulatory schedules rather than discretionary consumption, though cheaper diagnostics and reduced downtime could support some additional aviation activity. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate and the physical, regulated core persists, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Airline and commercial pilots
rationale: Piloting already relies heavily on automation, and AI can further improve flight planning, weather/routing decisions, system monitoring, communications support, and simulator training. However, the core job still requires certified human responsibility in a safety-critical, regulated, real-world environment involving takeoff, landing, emergencies, passenger trust, and coordination with ATC and crew. Demand would expand only modestly if pilot labor became cheaper because air travel is constrained by aircraft, fuel, airport capacity, regulation, and the fact that people do not take 10x more flights simply because cockpit labor is cheaper. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to remove the human-centered core over the next decade, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Animal care and service workers
rationale: The core work is hands-on, physical, and location-specific: feeding, cleaning, grooming, exercising, observing, restraining, and training live animals in unpredictable real-world settings. AI can help with scheduling, customer communication, recordkeeping, remote monitoring, behavior notes, and some automated feeders or cleaning tools, but it does not replace the central human-animal interaction or physical care. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper pet care, grooming, boarding, and training could lead owners to buy more services, especially as pets are increasingly treated as family members, but demand is still constrained by the number of pets and the need for trusted in-person care. Because disruption is low, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Announcers and DJs
rationale: A large share of broadcast announcing and radio DJ work is language-, audio-, and software-based: writing scripts, reading copy, selecting music, producing segments, doing promos, and engaging audiences online, all of which AI voice, generative writing, recommendation, and automation tools can already affect. Live event DJs and emcees are more resilient because they require physical presence, crowd reading, client interaction, and real-time social performance, but even there playlists, mixing, planning, and announcements can be partially automated. Demand elasticity is low because radio airtime, local advertising budgets, weddings, clubs, and events do not expand dramatically just because announcing or music hosting becomes cheaper. Given high disruption and limited ability for demand to absorb productivity gains, the occupation is likely to see replacement pressure, especially in broadcast and radio.

title: Anthropologists and archeologists
rationale: AI can substantially assist the digital and cognitive parts of this occupation, including literature review, transcription and translation, qualitative coding, GIS/remote-sensing analysis, artifact classification, database management, and report drafting. However, much of the core work still depends on field presence, excavation, site assessment, interviews, cultural interpretation, regulatory judgment, and building trust with communities or stakeholders, which limits full automation. Demand elasticity is relatively low because archeological compliance work is tied to construction activity and regulation, while academic and government research is funding-constrained; cheaper analysis may expand corporate and applied anthropology somewhat but not dramatically. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators
rationale: The occupation is heavily language-, document-, and judgment-based: AI can help review evidence, summarize claims, draft settlement language, research rules or precedents, and model possible resolutions. However, the core role also depends on perceived neutrality, legitimacy, emotional intelligence, and real-time management of conflict, which limits full automation, especially in high-stakes disputes. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper dispute resolution could unlock more low-value, consumer, workplace, family, and small-business disputes that are currently too costly to mediate, but total demand is constrained by the number of disputes, court or contract rules, public budgets, and parties’ willingness to accept AI-mediated outcomes. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is not strong enough to fully offset productivity gains, the occupation is likely to be restructured rather than broadly replaced or augmented.

title: Architects
rationale: Architects do substantial digital and cognitive work—CAD/BIM drawings, specifications, code research, cost estimates, design iteration, renderings, and documentation—that AI and generative design tools can materially accelerate. However, the occupation also depends on client trust, professional judgment, licensure and liability, coordination with engineers and contractors, and site visits, which limits full replacement. Demand could expand as cheaper architectural services make custom design, renovations, sustainability upgrades, and more design iterations accessible to more clients, but total demand is constrained by construction budgets, permitting, land use rules, and the fact that architecture is only one part of project cost. This points to restructuring: fewer hours spent on drafting and routine documentation, more emphasis on design direction, client management, code/liability oversight, and construction-process coordination.

title: Architectural and engineering managers
rationale: Architectural and engineering managers do largely cognitive and coordination-heavy work: planning projects, setting budgets and schedules, reviewing technical output, communicating with teams, and managing documentation, all of which AI tools can substantially accelerate. However, the role also depends on human leadership, accountability, personnel decisions, domain judgment, and coordination with physical construction, manufacturing, laboratory, or regulatory realities, so AI is unlikely to fully replace the core managerial function. Demand could expand somewhat as cheaper engineering and design workflows enable more R&D, infrastructure, and product-development activity, but it is constrained by capital budgets, regulation, construction timelines, and the need for real-world implementation. The result is substantial restructuring: managers will oversee more AI-augmented workflows and larger spans of technical output, while those who cannot adapt to AI-enabled planning, analysis, and supervision may be displaced.

title: Archivists, curators, and museum workers
rationale: AI can materially assist with archival description, metadata generation, OCR/transcription, search, provenance research, exhibit text, grant writing, and digital records management. However, much of the occupation still depends on expert judgment, institutional trust, physical object handling, conservation treatment, exhibit installation, donor relations, and public-facing work that requires human presence. Demand could expand moderately because many archives and museums have large backlogs of uncataloged or undigitized materials, but budgets, physical collections, and public funding constraints limit how much cheaper output translates into more jobs. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the entire occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Art directors
rationale: Art directors do largely cognitive, digital, and creative work—concept development, visual selection, layout/style direction, client presentation, and review of design output—which is directly affected by generative image, video, layout, and branding tools. AI can already accelerate mood boards, comps, visual variants, campaign personalization, and production review, though human taste, client management, leadership, and production judgment remain central. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper visual production enables more advertising variants, more digital content, more small-business branding, and faster experimentation across media channels. Because disruption is high but expanded demand for visual content is likely to absorb much of the productivity gain, the occupation is best categorized as augment rather than replace.

title: Assemblers and fabricators
rationale: Assemblers and fabricators do mostly physical, hands-on work involving positioning parts, using tools, soldering, welding, fitting, and performing in-person quality checks, so generative AI affects only limited schematic-reading, inspection, training, and workflow-support tasks. However, AI-enabled robotics, machine vision, and collaborative robots are increasingly relevant in structured factory settings and can automate some repetitive or delicate assembly work, keeping disruption at the high end of moderate. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because cheaper assembly may support some reshoring and growth in areas such as EV batteries or electronics, but demand for vehicles, appliances, machinery, and fabricated products is ultimately constrained by final-product demand and capital investment. Because the core job remains substantially physical and site-based, the occupation fits the resilient category despite ongoing automation pressure.

title: Athletes and sports competitors
rationale: The core work of athletes and sports competitors is embodied, physical, and performed live under unpredictable competitive conditions, so AI cannot substitute for the central task of competing for spectators. AI will meaningfully assist peripheral and preparatory tasks such as video analysis, opponent scouting, training optimization, injury prevention, and nutrition planning, but these tools augment rather than replace athletic performance. Demand is relatively inelastic because roster spots, league expansion, event schedules, and audience attention are structurally limited, even if training and analysis become cheaper. Because disruption is low, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Athletic trainers
rationale: Athletic trainers perform substantial hands-on, in-person work: taping and bracing, evaluating injuries on the field, providing first aid, guiding rehabilitation, and coordinating with athletes, coaches, parents, and physicians. AI can help with documentation, injury-risk analytics, wearable monitoring, concussion protocols, and generating rehab plans, but it does not replace the need for real-time clinical judgment and physical presence during practices and events. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper tools could expand access for schools, youth sports, aging recreational athletes, military, and smaller organizations that currently cannot afford robust coverage, though licensing, staffing ratios, and event-based presence limit unlimited scaling. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite useful AI augmentation, the occupation fits the resilient category.

title: Atmospheric scientists, including meteorologists
rationale: Atmospheric science is heavily data-, model-, code-, graphics-, and communication-based, and AI is already improving forecasting, nowcasting, climate modeling, report drafting, and visualization. Human expertise remains important for interpreting uncertain model outputs, issuing high-stakes warnings, conducting research, maintaining public trust, and handling some field or instrumentation work, so the occupation is not fully automatable. Demand can expand for hyperlocal forecasts, climate-risk analytics, logistics, agriculture, energy, insurance, and emergency-management applications, but much of the field is constrained by public funding and many basic forecasts are already widely available. This combination of high disruption and moderate demand expansion points to restructuring: fewer routine forecasting tasks, more emphasis on AI-enabled interpretation, domain judgment, communication, and specialized advisory work.

title: Audiologists
rationale: Audiology includes cognitive diagnostic work, test interpretation, treatment planning, documentation, and device fitting that AI can meaningfully assist through automated audiogram analysis, hearing-aid optimization, telehealth triage, and clinical note generation. However, much of the core work still requires licensed clinical judgment, in-person examination, patient counseling, pediatric or geriatric communication, vestibular assessment, and coordination with physicians or surgeons. Demand has moderate elasticity because hearing loss is underdiagnosed and an aging population plus cheaper screening and devices could expand access, but utilization is still constrained by healthcare reimbursement, patient adoption, and the need for clinical encounters. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment workflow and expand capacity than fundamentally replace the occupation.

title: Automotive body and glass repairers
rationale: Automotive body and glass repair is predominantly hands-on physical work involving inspection, disassembly, welding, sanding, frame alignment, glass removal, sealing, and installation in variable real-world conditions. AI can improve peripheral and semi-core tasks such as damage estimation, insurance documentation, parts ordering, repair planning, and sensor/calibration guidance, but it is unlikely to automate most shop-floor repair work over the next decade. Demand is relatively inelastic because the volume of work is mainly driven by accidents, wear, insurance decisions, and vehicle ownership rather than by the price of repair, although cheaper repairs could modestly increase cosmetic and marginal repairs. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and the core work remains physical and skilled, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Automotive service technicians and mechanics
rationale: AI can improve diagnostic workflows, interpret fault codes, recommend repair procedures, generate estimates, and document work, especially as vehicles become more software- and sensor-heavy. However, the core job remains hands-on inspection, disassembly, repair, replacement, calibration, and testing in a physical environment with varied vehicle conditions, which limits direct automation. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of repairs is tied to vehicles in use, mileage, accidents, wear, and maintenance schedules rather than the price of technician labor, though cheaper diagnostics may modestly expand preventative maintenance. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and the physical core remains essential, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Bakers
rationale: Baking is primarily hands-on physical work: measuring and handling ingredients, shaping dough, loading ovens, monitoring product quality, cleaning equipment, and working safely around heat and machinery. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as inventory, production planning, recipe scaling, scheduling, quality monitoring, and demand forecasting, and some commercial bakeries will continue automating production lines, but the core occupation still requires real-world manipulation and sensory judgment. Demand for baked goods would expand somewhat if production became cheaper, especially for specialty, customized, or fresher products, but food consumption is limited by population, diet, retail space, and price sensitivity rather than unlimited latent demand. Because disruption to the core daily work remains low-to-moderate, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists
rationale: The core work is hands-on, physical, and performed in close proximity to clients: cutting, coloring, styling, shaving, sanitation, and real-time adjustment to hair texture and client preferences. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as appointment scheduling, marketing, customer records, product recommendations, and virtual hairstyle visualization, but it is unlikely to replace the dexterous, trust-based service interaction at scale over the next decade. Demand would expand somewhat if services became cheaper or faster, especially for coloring, styling, and premium treatments, but basic haircut demand is constrained by hair growth, time, and in-person service capacity. Because disruption to the core occupation is low, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Bartenders
rationale: Bartending is primarily in-person, physical, and social work: mixing and serving drinks, checking IDs, monitoring intoxication, handling cash or tabs, cleaning, restocking, and managing customer interactions in a real-world setting. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as inventory forecasting, scheduling, menu recommendations, POS automation, and training, and some robotic drink systems may appear in high-volume or novelty venues, but the core hospitality and responsibility functions remain human-centered. Demand would expand only modestly if labor became cheaper because alcohol consumption and bar visits are limited by time, regulation, venue capacity, health concerns, and the fact that customers often pay for atmosphere and service rather than just drink production. Because disruption is low-to-moderate, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite some automation at the margins.

title: Bill and account collectors
rationale: Bill and account collection is heavily phone-, text-, database-, and script-based work, with core tasks such as skip tracing, debtor outreach, recordkeeping, compliance scripting, and repayment-plan negotiation directly addressable by AI voice agents and workflow automation. AI can already prioritize accounts, generate compliant messages, summarize calls, update systems, and increasingly conduct routine negotiations with human escalation only for difficult cases. Demand elasticity is low because the stock of delinquent accounts is finite, collection contacts are legally constrained, and cheaper collection does not create much new socially or commercially desired activity beyond pursuing smaller balances. Because disruption is very high and demand expansion is limited, productivity gains are likely to translate mainly into fewer collectors rather than much more employment.

title: Biochemists and biophysicists
rationale: AI is already materially changing biochemistry and biophysics through protein-structure prediction, molecular design, literature synthesis, image analysis, omics analysis, experiment planning, and automated report or grant drafting. The disruption score is tempered by the fact that core work still depends on wet-lab experimentation, physical instrumentation, safety protocols, biological validation, and interdisciplinary judgment. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster biological research would unlock more drug discovery, diagnostics, synthetic biology, agricultural biotech, and environmental applications, although clinical trials, regulation, lab capacity, and funding constraints limit unlimited expansion. Because disruption is high but expanded research output is likely to absorb much of the productivity gain, the occupation is best categorized as augment.

title: Bioengineers and biomedical engineers
rationale: Biomedical engineering includes substantial AI-exposed knowledge work: literature review, statistical modeling, simulation, software development, design optimization, documentation, and analysis of biological or device data. However, the occupation also requires hands-on experimentation, prototyping, validation, clinical interaction, manufacturing coordination, and regulatory judgment, which limits full automation. Demand for biomedical devices, diagnostics, prosthetics, implants, and personalized medical technologies would expand if design and analysis became cheaper, but growth is constrained by clinical testing, regulation, reimbursement, manufacturing, and adoption cycles. Because disruption is high but demand elasticity is only moderate, AI is likely to substantially restructure the work rather than simply eliminate or broadly expand headcount.

title: Biological technicians
rationale: Biological technicians do a mix of hands-on wet-lab work, sample preparation, equipment maintenance, observation, documentation, and data analysis, so AI will materially affect the digital and analytical parts but not eliminate the need for physical laboratory presence. AI tools and lab automation can improve experimental design, image analysis, recordkeeping, anomaly detection, and interpretation, but many tasks still require manual sample handling, compliance with protocols, and troubleshooting real instruments and biological materials. Demand elasticity is fairly high because cheaper, faster experimentation would likely increase the volume of biotech, pharmaceutical, environmental, agricultural, and synthetic biology research. Because disruption is meaningful but still capped by the occupation’s hands-on laboratory core, the net effect is resilient rather than replace, restructure, or augment.

title: Boilermakers
rationale: Boilermakers perform mostly physical, site-specific work involving installation, welding, alignment, inspection, cleaning, and repair in hazardous, cramped, and variable environments. AI may help with blueprint interpretation, scheduling, predictive maintenance, robotic welding, and inspection tools, but it does not replace the core hands-on field work over the next decade. Demand is relatively inelastic because the need is tied to the installed base of boilers, tanks, pressure vessels, and industrial facilities, and cheaper labor would not cause customers to build or maintain vastly more of them. Because disruption is low-to-moderate, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite weak demand growth.

title: Bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks
rationale: This occupation is highly exposed because most core tasks are digital, rules-based, and data-oriented: entering transactions, coding accounts, reconciling records, producing reports, and checking postings for errors. Modern accounting platforms, bank feeds, OCR, automated categorization, anomaly detection, and generative AI assistants already automate or accelerate much of this work, leaving humans mainly for exceptions, oversight, client communication, and judgment calls. Demand elasticity is low because the amount of bookkeeping needed is largely tied to the number of businesses and transactions, not to the price of clerical labor, though cheaper tools may bring some underserved small firms into better compliance. Because disruption is very high and demand expansion is limited, the net effect is replacement, with fewer clerks needed and remaining roles shifting toward review and advisory support.

title: Broadcast, sound, and video technicians
rationale: AI and automation can materially affect the digital portions of this occupation, including audio cleanup, mixing, video editing, lighting control, captioning, signal monitoring, and some broadcast operations. However, a large share of the work still involves physical setup, teardown, cabling, installation, live-event presence, equipment maintenance, and real-time troubleshooting in unpredictable venues, which limits full automation. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper production and AV operation could expand podcasts, livestreams, corporate video, digital signage, and small-event production, but live events, broadcast schedules, and venue-based work are not unlimited. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with AI changing tools and staffing ratios more than replacing the core role outright.

title: Budget analysts
rationale: Budget analysts perform largely digital, cognitive work: consolidating spreadsheets, reviewing proposals for completeness and compliance, forecasting needs, analyzing tradeoffs, monitoring variances, and drafting reports. AI can already assist substantially with data cleaning, scenario modeling, anomaly detection, cost-benefit summaries, compliance checks, and written explanations, although human judgment remains important for organizational politics, accountability, and defending recommendations. Demand is relatively inelastic because most organizations have a fixed budgeting cycle and a limited number of funding decisions; cheaper analysis may enable more scenarios and monitoring but not a dramatic increase in budget analyst headcount. With high disruption and low elasticity, productivity gains are likely to reduce the number of analysts needed rather than create enough new demand to offset automation.

title: Bus drivers
rationale: Bus driving is a real-world, safety-critical physical job involving traffic judgment, passenger supervision, disability assistance, incident response, and regulatory compliance, so current AI mainly affects routing, scheduling, dispatch, and driver-assistance systems rather than replacing the driver. Autonomous bus technology is relevant, especially on fixed routes or geofenced shuttle services, but mixed traffic, bad weather, liability, school-child supervision, and public-sector procurement make broad deployment over the next decade uncertain. Demand would expand somewhat if service became cheaper, through more frequent transit, rural routes, paratransit, and intercity service, but total need is constrained by population, school enrollment, commuting patterns, public budgets, and road capacity. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high for the occupation as a whole, the net effect is resilient despite some longer-term automation risk.

title: Butchers
rationale: Butchery is primarily physical, hands-on work involving cutting, deboning, grinding, wrapping, cleaning, lifting, and maintaining sanitation in a real-world food environment. AI may help with peripheral tasks such as inventory forecasting, ordering, scheduling, pricing, or sales trend analysis, and robotics may automate some standardized meat-processing tasks, but most retail butcher work still requires dexterity, judgment, and physical presence. Demand elasticity is low because consumers are unlikely to buy dramatically more meat simply because cutting and packaging become faster or cheaper, and demand is constrained by diet, household consumption, and retail food patterns. Because disruption to the core occupation is low, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite limited long-term demand growth.

title: Calibration technologists and technicians
rationale: Calibration technologists and technicians do use digital records, test data, standards documentation, and diagnostic reasoning that AI can assist with, especially in report generation, scheduling, anomaly detection, and interpreting calibration histories. However, the core work remains hands-on: inspecting physical instruments, connecting test equipment, making adjustments, working in labs or plants, and applying metrology judgment in real-world settings. Demand is only moderately elastic because much calibration is driven by compliance, safety, quality-control schedules, and the installed base of equipment rather than by discretionary consumption, though cheaper calibration could expand testing of lower-value sensors and automated systems. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment tools and workflows than fundamentally replace the occupation.

title: Cardiovascular technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can meaningfully assist with EKG interpretation, signal quality checks, anomaly detection, documentation, and summarizing findings for physicians. However, much of the occupation involves hands-on patient preparation, positioning, equipment operation, monitoring during procedures, and responding in clinical settings, which require physical presence and healthcare-team coordination. Demand would expand somewhat with an aging population and cheaper screening, but it is constrained by physician referrals, insurance coverage, facility capacity, and the fact that patients will not consume unlimited cardiac or pulmonary tests. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment workflow than replace the core role.

title: Career and technical education teachers
rationale: AI can materially assist CTE teachers with lesson planning, quizzes, grading, tutoring support, simulations, and adapting explanations for different learners. However, the core of many CTE programs involves hands-on demonstration, safety supervision, tool and equipment use, lab management, credentialed instruction, and in-person coaching, which limits full automation. Demand could expand somewhat through cheaper vocational training, adult reskilling, and AI-enhanced simulations, but public-school budgets, enrollment trends, facilities, equipment, and certification requirements constrain how much headcount grows. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the occupation’s hands-on core, the net effect is resilient.

title: Carpenters
rationale: Carpentry is primarily hands-on, physical work performed in varied and often unpredictable jobsites, involving measuring, cutting, lifting, fitting, installing, and adjusting materials onsite. AI can help with estimating, blueprint interpretation, scheduling, layout, augmented-reality guidance, and prefabrication workflows, but it does not directly replace most core manual tasks over the next decade. Demand has moderate elasticity because lower construction and remodeling costs could unlock some additional housing, renovations, and commercial projects, but land, permitting, materials, financing, and local construction constraints limit expansion. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite useful peripheral tools, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Cartographers and photogrammetrists
rationale: Cartography and photogrammetry are heavily digital, data-intensive occupations involving GIS, remote sensing, image interpretation, feature extraction, map design, and data integration, all of which are directly affected by AI, computer vision, and automated geospatial workflows. AI can increasingly automate classification of satellite and LiDAR imagery, change detection, map updating, and visualization, though human judgment remains important for accuracy, context, validation, client needs, and some field verification. Demand should expand moderately because cheaper mapping enables more frequent updates, richer geospatial layers, disaster planning, climate analysis, infrastructure monitoring, and private-sector location intelligence, but much employment is tied to government and project budgets that limit unconstrained growth. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is likely moderate rather than explosive, the occupation is best categorized as restructure.

title: Cashiers
rationale: Cashier work is highly routine transaction processing, and the core tasks of scanning items, taking payment, issuing receipts, and handling basic customer prompts are already being automated through self-checkout, mobile checkout, online ordering, and increasingly computer-vision or AI-assisted retail systems. The job still includes physical presence, bagging, age checks, returns, customer assistance, and store upkeep, which keeps disruption below the maximum. Demand for cashier labor is quite inelastic: cheaper checkout does not cause consumers to buy dramatically more groceries, fuel, or retail goods, so productivity gains mainly reduce staffing needs rather than expand output. Because disruption is high and elasticity is low, the occupation fits the replace category.

title: Chefs and head cooks
rationale: Chefs and head cooks have some AI-exposed tasks, including menu ideation, recipe development, purchasing, inventory, scheduling, pricing, and social media promotion. However, the core job remains highly embodied and on-site: tasting and smelling food, supervising a fast-moving kitchen, judging ingredient quality, handling equipment, maintaining sanitation, and responding to real-time service problems. Demand could expand moderately if AI lowers costs through better planning and automation, but restaurant demand is constrained by meal occasions, location, labor, hospitality, and consumers’ desire for human-led dining experiences. Because disruption is low-to-moderate rather than high, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Chemical engineers
rationale: Chemical engineering has substantial cognitive and digital components—process modeling, simulation, literature review, cost estimation, compliance documentation, and design optimization—that AI can accelerate meaningfully. However, the core work remains tied to physical plants, laboratory validation, safety-critical decisions, equipment constraints, and regulatory accountability, so AI is more likely to augment engineers than fully absorb the occupation. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper engineering could enable more process optimization, materials development, and sustainability projects, but total demand is constrained by capital-intensive manufacturing, product-market demand, and regulation. Because disruption is significant but not high enough to replace the hands-on and safety-critical core, the occupation fits the resilient category.

title: Chemical technicians
rationale: Chemical technicians perform a mix of hands-on laboratory and manufacturing tasks—preparing solutions, operating instruments, maintaining equipment, handling samples, and troubleshooting processes—so much of the core work still requires physical presence and procedural judgment. AI can materially assist with data analysis, interpreting test results, documentation, report generation, quality monitoring, and experiment planning, but it does not easily replace the embodied lab work and safety-sensitive equipment handling. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper and faster testing could expand environmental monitoring, product quality testing, materials R&D, and compliance work, though it remains limited by physical samples, production volumes, regulation, and lab capacity. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Chemists and materials scientists
rationale: Chemists and materials scientists combine hands-on laboratory work with substantial cognitive tasks such as literature review, experimental design, molecular or materials modeling, data analysis, and technical reporting, many of which are directly affected by AI. Over the next decade, AI-driven simulation, generative molecule/material design, automated analysis, and robotic labs are likely to change how research and testing are performed, although physical experimentation, safety, instrumentation, and scale-up constraints keep this from being fully automatable. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper discovery and analysis would unlock more R&D in drugs, batteries, semiconductors, biomaterials, and quality testing, but demand is limited by regulation, capital-intensive labs, manufacturing constraints, and the need for real-world validation. The result is restructuring: the occupation remains important, but workers will need to shift toward AI-enabled experimental strategy, validation, instrumentation oversight, and interdisciplinary interpretation.

title: Childcare workers
rationale: Childcare work is dominated by in-person supervision, safety monitoring, feeding, diapering, hygiene, emotional support, and managing unpredictable child behavior, all of which require trusted human presence and physical responsiveness. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as lesson planning, parent communication, developmental documentation, scheduling, and camera-assisted monitoring, but it does not meaningfully replace the core caregiving role over the next decade. Demand is moderately elastic because childcare is expensive and cheaper provision could increase usage, work hours, and access for families, but birth rates, licensing rules, staff-child ratios, and parental trust limit expansion. Because disruption is low, the occupation is best categorized as resilient despite some AI-enabled administrative augmentation.

title: Chiropractors
rationale: Chiropractors’ core work is hands-on, in-person assessment and manual manipulation of the spine and musculoskeletal system, which current AI cannot directly perform. AI can help with documentation, scheduling, patient intake, imaging support, exercise recommendations, and marketing, but these are peripheral or decision-support tasks rather than the central service. Demand has moderate elasticity because lower administrative costs and better triage could expand access to pain-management and wellness care, especially for aging patients, but treatment still requires physical appointments and is constrained by patient need, insurance, and trust. Because disruption is low-to-moderate, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Civil engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: AI will materially affect the office-based portions of this job, including CAD drafting, plan review support, quantity takeoffs, cost estimating, report preparation, file management, and analysis of survey or sensor data. However, a substantial share of the role still involves field presence: observing construction, collecting site data, testing materials and soils, troubleshooting conditions, and coordinating with engineers and contractors in unpredictable physical environments. Demand elasticity is limited because infrastructure projects are constrained mainly by public budgets, permitting, construction capacity, and engineering approval requirements rather than the cost of technician labor alone. Because disruption is significant but not high enough to fully reshape the occupation’s physical and site-based core, the net effect is resilient.

title: Civil engineers
rationale: Civil engineering includes substantial digital and cognitive work—CAD/BIM design, calculations, permitting documents, cost estimates, code research, and report writing—that AI can materially accelerate. However, the occupation remains tied to licensed professional judgment, public safety liability, site-specific conditions, construction coordination, inspections, and interaction with contractors and agencies, limiting full automation. Demand is only moderately elastic because infrastructure needs are large but constrained by public funding, permitting, land use, and construction capacity, and engineering labor is only one part of total project cost. Because disruption is meaningful but not enough to reshape the entire occupation’s core around AI, the net effect is resilient rather than replacement or restructuring.

title: Claims adjusters, appraisers, examiners, and investigators
rationale: Claims work contains a large share of digital and cognitive tasks: reviewing policies and records, evaluating documentation and photos, estimating losses, detecting fraud patterns, drafting reports, and authorizing or denying payments. AI and computer vision can already automate parts of damage appraisal, claims triage, document review, fraud scoring, and settlement recommendation, although human judgment, negotiation, field inspection, and complex investigations remain important. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of claims is driven mainly by insured events, policy coverage, and disasters rather than by the cost of claims processing. With high disruption and limited demand expansion, productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount and concentrate human work in complex, contested, or field-intensive claims.

title: Clinical laboratory technologists and technicians
rationale: AI and laboratory automation can materially affect parts of this occupation, especially automated result validation, abnormality detection in images or blood smears, workflow triage, quality control, and data entry into medical records. However, much of the core work still involves physical specimen handling, wet-lab procedures, equipment calibration and troubleshooting, biohazard protocols, and regulated clinical accountability, which limits full AI substitution. Demand has moderate elasticity: cheaper and faster testing could expand preventive screening, genetic testing, chronic disease monitoring, and access in underserved settings, but utilization is constrained by physician orders, reimbursement, clinical guidelines, and patient need. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Coaches and scouts
rationale: AI will materially affect video analysis, opponent scouting, player statistics, training-plan design, and recruiting databases, especially at college and professional levels. However, much of coaching remains in-person, physical, relational, and motivational: running practices, correcting technique, managing team culture, ensuring safety, and making context-rich decisions during competition. Demand could expand moderately as cheaper analytics and personalized training tools make higher-quality instruction available to more youth, recreational, and amateur athletes, but many jobs are constrained by school/team budgets and the need for human supervision. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the core occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Community health workers
rationale: AI can materially assist community health workers with documentation, translation, scheduling, resource matching, benefits navigation, educational materials, and identifying at-risk clients. However, the core work depends heavily on in-person outreach, trust, cultural competence, empathy, home and community presence, and coordination with local providers, so AI reshapes support tasks more than it replaces the occupation. Demand elasticity is relatively high because unmet need for health navigation, chronic disease support, behavioral health support, and social-service access is substantial, especially in underserved communities, though funding and human-trust constraints limit unlimited expansion. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Compensation and benefits managers
rationale: This occupation is heavily digital and analytical: compensation benchmarking, benefits-cost analysis, compliance monitoring, policy drafting, employee communications, and presentation preparation are all areas where AI can materially improve or automate workflows. However, the role also includes senior stakeholder management, vendor selection, budget accountability, and judgment about organizational strategy, so AI is more likely to absorb large portions of staff and analytical work than fully replace executive decision-making. Demand elasticity is low because most organizations need only a limited amount of compensation and benefits oversight, and making analysis cheaper does not create many more firms or employees needing plans. With high disruption and limited demand expansion, productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount or consolidate work into fewer managers and outsourced platforms, fitting the replace category.

title: Compensation, benefits, and job analysis specialists
rationale: This occupation is predominantly digital, analytical, and language-based: specialists compare compensation data, interpret policies and regulations, draft job descriptions, prepare reports, and make recommendations. AI can already automate or strongly assist with salary benchmarking, benefits-plan comparisons, compliance monitoring, job classification, report drafting, and employee-facing explanations, though humans remain important for accountability, sensitive judgments, and stakeholder management. Demand elasticity is limited because most organizations need a bounded amount of compensation and benefits work tied to their workforce size and regulatory obligations; cheaper analysis may enable more frequent audits or help smaller firms, but it is unlikely to create proportional new demand. With high disruption and relatively low elasticity, productivity gains are likely to reduce the number of specialists needed per organization, making the net effect replace.

title: Compliance officers
rationale: Compliance work is heavily cognitive, document-based, and language-intensive: tracking regulations, drafting policies, reviewing records, preparing reports, risk scoring, and creating training materials are all tasks AI can materially accelerate. Some responsibilities still require human judgment, organizational authority, interviews, investigations, and occasional onsite presence, but much of the routine monitoring and documentation layer is in AI’s direct path. Demand is only modestly elastic because compliance is largely driven by legal requirements, audits, and organizational risk tolerance rather than open-ended consumer demand; cheaper compliance may expand monitoring for smaller firms and continuous controls, but not enough to absorb large productivity gains. With high disruption and relatively low elasticity, the occupation is likely to see significant automation of routine roles and a shift toward fewer, more senior human compliance overseers.

title: Computer and information research scientists
rationale: Computer and information research scientists do almost entirely digital, cognitive work: coding, modeling, experiment design, data analysis, technical writing, and literature synthesis, all of which are directly affected by current AI tools. AI can substantially accelerate prototyping, code generation, simulation, paper drafting, and exploration of research ideas, although humans remain important for problem selection, validation, scientific judgment, and cross-disciplinary framing. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper research and development would likely lead firms, universities, government agencies, and startups to pursue many more computing, AI, cybersecurity, robotics, and data-intensive projects. Because disruption is very high but cheaper output is likely to expand the frontier of technology creation rather than simply reduce fixed demand, the net effect is best classified as augment.

title: Computer and information systems managers
rationale: Computer and information systems managers do predominantly digital, cognitive work, and AI can materially assist with project planning, cost-benefit analysis, system monitoring, cybersecurity triage, documentation, vendor comparison, and technical decision support. However, the core role also involves organizational judgment, accountability, leadership, personnel decisions, budgeting tradeoffs, and coordination with executives and vendors, which keeps disruption below the most automatable digital occupations. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster IT planning and management would likely lead organizations to undertake more cloud, cybersecurity, AI, automation, and digital-platform projects rather than simply consume a fixed amount of IT oversight. The net effect is augment: AI will change the skill mix and expand managerial span, but growing technological complexity and AI adoption should create enough additional demand for capable IT managers to keep employment stable or growing.

title: Computer hardware engineers
rationale: Computer hardware engineering is highly cognitive and tool-mediated: schematic design, simulation, verification, test analysis, documentation, and hardware-software co-design are all areas where AI-enabled EDA, code generation, design-space exploration, and debugging assistants can materially change workflows. The occupation is not fully automatable because physical prototyping, lab validation, manufacturing constraints, safety/reliability requirements, and cross-functional engineering judgment remain central. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster hardware design would unlock more custom chips, embedded systems, AI accelerators, IoT devices, automotive electronics, and medical/device applications, although fabrication costs and supply-chain constraints limit unlimited expansion. Because disruption is high but cheaper design is likely to create substantially more hardware development rather than simply reduce staffing, the net effect is augment.

title: Computer network architects
rationale: Computer network architects do predominantly digital, analytical work: designing network topologies, generating documentation, configuring systems, analyzing performance data, and troubleshooting, all of which AI and automation tools can materially accelerate. However, the role still requires human judgment around security, reliability, vendor constraints, organizational requirements, physical infrastructure, and accountability for outages or implementation risk. Demand should expand meaningfully because cloud migration, AI workloads, cybersecurity needs, and network modernization all increase the need for better architecture, but growth is constrained by hardware budgets, enterprise change cycles, and the finite number of networks organizations need. This fits restructure: AI will substantially change workflows and skill requirements, but demand expansion is likely enough to prevent a simple replacement outcome.

title: Computer programmers
rationale: Computer programming is almost entirely digital, language- and logic-based work, and AI coding tools already assist with code generation, debugging, testing, refactoring, and documentation. Demand for software is fairly elastic because cheaper programming enables more internal tools, automation, customization, and maintenance work, but the specific occupation of computer programmer is constrained by task consolidation into software developer roles and automation of routine coding. The net effect is restructure: AI will not eliminate the need for programming expertise, but it will substantially change the job toward specification, integration, review, testing, and higher-level problem solving while reducing demand for workers focused mainly on translating designs into code.

title: Computer support specialists
rationale: Computer support work is heavily digital, language-based, and procedural: diagnosing user problems, documenting tickets, guiding users step-by-step, and escalating cases are all tasks that AI chatbots, copilots, and automated remediation tools can already handle for many common issues. Some onsite hardware setup, network troubleshooting, and complex enterprise incidents still require human judgment or physical presence, but a large share of tier-1 and routine support is directly automatable. Demand is only weakly elastic because the volume of support is largely tied to the number of users, devices, and incidents rather than a desire to consume much more support when it becomes cheaper. Because disruption is high and cheaper support is likely to reduce staffing needs more than it expands demand, the net effect is replace.

title: Computer systems analysts
rationale: Computer systems analysts perform predominantly digital, cognitive work: requirements analysis, system design, cost-benefit analysis, testing, documentation, and some programming, all of which AI tools can materially accelerate. However, the role also depends on organizational context, stakeholder communication, change management, and translating business needs into workable systems, which limits full automation. Demand elasticity is high because many organizations have large backlogs of modernization, integration, cybersecurity, cloud, data, and AI-adoption projects that become more feasible if analysis and implementation planning get cheaper. Because disruption is high but cheaper work is likely to unlock substantial additional IT transformation demand, the occupation is best classified as augment.

title: Concierges
rationale: AI chatbots, voice agents, booking tools, recommendation systems, and building-management software can automate many concierge tasks such as answering routine questions, making reservations, arranging transportation, handling emails, and routing maintenance requests. However, the occupation still relies heavily on in-person hospitality, greeting residents or guests, handling packages, resolving ambiguous interpersonal issues, and providing a reassuring physical presence, especially in residential and senior-living settings. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper concierge-like services could expand to more buildings and lower-end hotels, but on-site staffing is constrained by the number of properties and the premium placed on human service. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to eliminate the physical and interpersonal core, the occupation fits the resilient category.

title: Conservation scientists and foresters
rationale: AI will materially affect the analytical and office-based parts of this occupation, including GIS mapping, remote-sensing interpretation, forest inventory estimation, fire-risk modeling, compliance documentation, and management-plan drafting. However, much of the core work still requires field judgment, travel to remote sites, stakeholder negotiation, supervision of crews, regulatory accountability, and participation in activities such as fire suppression or habitat restoration. Demand could expand moderately because cheaper monitoring and planning would allow more landowners and agencies to assess forests, rangelands, wildfire risk, water quality, and habitat conditions, but total demand is constrained by public budgets, land area, permitting, and implementation capacity. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to replace the field-based and supervisory core, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Construction and building inspectors
rationale: AI can materially assist the office and cognitive parts of inspection work, including code lookup, plan review, report drafting, photo analysis, scheduling, and remote inspection workflows. However, the core job still depends heavily on physical site presence, practical construction knowledge, use of testing equipment, judgment in ambiguous field conditions, and legally accountable enforcement decisions. Demand elasticity is low because inspection volume is largely tied to construction activity, permitting rules, real estate transactions, and safety regulations rather than the price of inspection labor. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to streamline and partially reshape the role than replace the occupation at scale.

title: Construction equipment operators
rationale: Construction equipment operation is primarily physical, site-specific work involving heavy machinery, coordination with crews, safety judgment, maintenance, and adaptation to changing terrain and weather. AI, GPS grade control, sensors, teleoperation, and semi-autonomous equipment will improve productivity and may automate some repetitive grading, hauling, paving, or mining tasks, but widespread full autonomy on varied construction sites remains difficult over the next decade. Demand would expand only modestly if operation became cheaper because construction is constrained by infrastructure budgets, permitting, materials, land, and project timelines rather than operator labor alone. Because AI affects important tools but does not fully reshape the hands-on core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Construction laborers and helpers
rationale: Construction laborers and helpers perform mostly physical, site-specific tasks such as moving materials, cleaning hazards, digging, assembling temporary structures, and assisting tradesworkers in unpredictable real-world environments. AI may improve scheduling, safety monitoring, surveying, equipment control, prefab logistics, and some robotic tools, but it does not directly replace the core hands-on labor at most jobsites over the next decade. Demand elasticity is relatively high because cheaper construction labor could unlock more housing, renovation, infrastructure repair, and commercial building, though permitting, land, materials, and financing limit expansion. Because disruption is low despite meaningful latent demand, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Construction managers
rationale: AI will materially improve construction managers' digital and cognitive tasks, including cost estimation, scheduling, contract review, progress reporting, procurement analysis, BIM coordination, and risk forecasting. However, the core job still depends heavily on onsite presence, judgment under changing physical conditions, leadership of subcontractors, client and inspector coordination, and responsibility for safety, delays, and emergencies. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper project management can support more renovations, infrastructure work, and smaller projects, but construction volume is constrained by land, permits, financing, materials, and skilled trades labor. Because disruption is significant but not high enough to remove the human-centered onsite coordination role, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Cooks
rationale: Cooking is primarily hands-on work involving food handling, heat, timing, dexterity, cleaning, safety, and real-time coordination in a physical kitchen, so current AI affects mostly peripheral tasks such as recipe planning, inventory, scheduling, and order routing. Robotics and automated cooking systems are more relevant in standardized fast food, cafeteria, and short-order settings, but they are less capable in varied restaurant kitchens that require adaptation, sensory judgment, and human presence. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper prepared food could increase takeout, delivery, institutional meals, and customized meal services, but total food consumption is naturally limited and restaurants also sell service, convenience, and experience. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate for the occupation as a whole, the net effect is resilient despite some automation pressure in fast food and highly standardized kitchens.

title: Correctional officers and bailiffs
rationale: Correctional officers and bailiffs perform work that is heavily tied to physical presence, legal authority, supervision, searches, escorts, restraint, and rapid response to unpredictable human behavior. AI can improve surveillance, incident detection, contraband screening, report writing, scheduling, and risk assessment, but these tools mostly support rather than replace the core custody and courtroom-security functions. Demand is highly inelastic because staffing needs are driven by inmate counts, court activity, law, safety rules, and government budgets; making the work cheaper would not cause society to consume many more jail or courtroom security services. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite low elasticity, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Cost estimators
rationale: Cost estimating is heavily digital and analytical: reading plans, extracting quantities, comparing databases, calculating labor/material costs, preparing bids, and writing reports are all tasks that AI-enabled estimating, BIM, CAD, and document-analysis tools can increasingly automate. Human judgment, site visits, contractor coordination, and handling unusual project conditions still matter, but much of the daily workflow is in AI's direct path. Demand elasticity is low because the number of construction, manufacturing, and repair projects does not expand proportionally just because estimates become cheaper, though firms may run more scenarios or serve smaller bids. With high disruption and limited demand expansion, productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount rather than be fully absorbed by new demand.

title: Court reporters and simultaneous captioners
rationale: The core work is converting speech into accurate text, speaker labels, timestamps, and searchable transcripts, which is almost entirely language-based and already directly affected by automatic speech recognition, diarization, and AI editing tools. Human workers will still be needed in high-stakes legal settings to certify, monitor, correct, and handle unclear audio, objections, gestures, and procedural context, but much of the capture and first-draft transcription work can be automated. Demand is only modestly elastic: cheaper transcription may increase captioning for meetings, online video, classes, and accessibility use cases, but court and deposition volumes are relatively fixed and many new uses will be served by self-service AI rather than occupational headcount. Because disruption is very high and demand expansion for human reporters/captioners is limited, the likely net effect is replacement with a smaller group of workers focused on verification, certification, and exception handling.

title: Craft and fine artists
rationale: AI image generators and design tools can materially affect ideation, sketching, illustration, portfolio development, marketing copy, grant applications, and some digital-art workflows. However, much of this occupation still involves hands-on manipulation of physical materials, studio practice, client/gallery relationships, and the market value of human authorship, provenance, and reputation. Demand could expand for cheaper visual concepts, decorative images, and customized designs, but demand for original fine art and handmade craft is constrained by income, taste, scarcity, and physical production. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough across the broad occupation to replace the physical and reputation-based core, the net effect is resilient.

title: Credit counselors
rationale: Credit counseling is largely language- and analysis-based: gathering financial information, assessing debts and budgets, explaining options, drafting plans, and communicating with creditors are all tasks AI can substantially assist or partially automate. Human judgment, trust-building, empathy with distressed clients, and some negotiation or referral work still matter, so the occupation is not fully automatable. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper counseling could reach many people who currently do not receive personalized debt, student loan, or budgeting help, but the total need is still bounded by debt distress, institutional programs, and clients' willingness or ability to engage. Because disruption is high while demand expansion is meaningful but not enough to fully absorb productivity gains, the occupation is likely to restructure rather than simply grow or disappear.

title: Customer service representatives
rationale: Customer service is heavily language- and software-mediated, with core tasks such as answering questions, processing routine requests, recording interactions, and handling billing or account changes directly in the path of chatbots, voice agents, and workflow automation. AI already performs many simple support interactions and is improving quickly on multi-turn troubleshooting, sentiment handling, and integration with customer databases, though humans remain important for complex, regulated, or emotionally sensitive escalations. Demand elasticity is low because customer service is largely a cost center tied to the size of a firm’s customer base; cheaper service may enable more 24/7 support and proactive outreach, but firms are unlikely to consume enough extra support labor to offset automation. Because disruption is high and demand expansion is limited, the occupation is likely to see significant headcount contraction with remaining roles focused on escalations, supervision, and exception handling.

title: Dancers and choreographers
rationale: Most core dancer work is embodied, physical, collaborative, and often tied to live performance, rehearsal, teaching, or audience presence, which limits direct AI substitution. AI can materially affect choreography ideation, video production, virtual performers, marketing, music selection, and online dance content, so choreographers and media-facing dancers face more change than purely live performers. Demand could expand moderately as cheaper AI-assisted production creates more dance videos, social media content, and instructional material, but live venues, arts funding, and the premium on human performance constrain headcount growth. Because disruption remains below the high-disruption threshold for the occupation as a whole, the net effect is resilient.

title: Data scientists
rationale: Data science is almost entirely digital, analytical, coding- and communication-based work, so AI directly affects core tasks such as data cleaning, exploratory analysis, model development, visualization, documentation, and even recommendation drafting. Current AI tools and AutoML systems already make many routine modeling and coding tasks faster, though humans remain important for problem framing, data governance, causal reasoning, domain judgment, and stakeholder trust.
