Demand elasticity is high because many organizations have far more data and potential analytics use cases than they can currently afford to pursue, and cheaper data science should expand experimentation, personalization, forecasting, and AI deployment. Because disruption is very high but cheaper output is likely to unlock substantial additional demand, the occupation is best classified as augment rather than replace.

title: Database administrators and architects
rationale: Database administration and architecture are highly digital, code- and systems-oriented occupations, and AI can already assist with SQL generation, schema design, query tuning, anomaly detection, documentation, migration planning, and troubleshooting. However, production reliability, security, compliance, legacy-system context, and cross-team tradeoffs still require expert human judgment, especially for architecture and incident response. Demand will expand as organizations build more AI-ready data infrastructure and manage larger, more complex datasets, but routine administration is also being compressed by cloud platforms, automation, and managed database services. The result is substantial task change and a shift from hands-on maintenance toward architecture, governance, security, and integration, making the net effect best classified as restructure.

title: Delivery truck drivers and driver/sales workers
rationale: AI already improves routing, dispatching, delivery confirmation, customer communication, and sales prompts, and autonomous-driving technology could affect parts of the job over the next decade. However, the core work still requires real-world driving in complex local environments, loading and unloading cargo, handling exceptions, and interacting with customers, making full automation difficult and uneven. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster delivery would likely expand e-commerce, same-day delivery, grocery, restaurant, and business-to-business delivery volumes. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite meaningful AI-enabled efficiency gains.

title: Dental and ophthalmic laboratory technicians and medical appliance technicians
rationale: AI and adjacent digital manufacturing tools can materially affect the CAD/CAM design, prescription interpretation, production planning, and quality-inspection parts of this work, especially in dental labs and automated ophthalmic lens production. However, the core occupation still involves physical fabrication, finishing, polishing, repair, material handling, and machine operation for customized medical products, which limits full AI substitution over the next decade. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper production could expand access to dental restorations, orthotics, prosthetics, and extra eyewear, but medical need, insurance coverage, prescriptions, and replacement cycles constrain unlimited growth. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation fits the resilient category despite ongoing automation pressure.

title: Dental assistants
rationale: Dental assistants' core work is hands-on, chairside, and patient-facing: preparing rooms, sterilizing instruments, passing tools, suctioning, positioning x-rays, and calming patients. AI can help with scheduling, billing, documentation, patient reminders, and possibly image-quality checks, but these are peripheral or supervisory rather than replacements for in-person clinical assistance. Demand is somewhat constrained by the volume of dental visits, dentist and hygienist capacity, insurance coverage, and patients' willingness to seek care, so cheaper assistant-related workflows would not create a dramatic expansion in demand. Because disruption to the core occupation is low, the role is best classified as resilient.

title: Dental hygienists
rationale: Dental hygienists’ core work is hands-on clinical care: removing plaque and tartar, applying sealants and fluoride, taking x-rays, and working precisely inside patients’ mouths. AI can assist with peripheral and cognitive tasks such as documentation, patient education, scheduling, and possibly x-ray interpretation, but it does not substantially automate the fine motor, in-person preventive care that defines the occupation. Demand could expand somewhat if administrative costs fall and access improves, especially with aging populations and broader preventive-care efforts, but cleaning frequency, insurance coverage, physical appointment capacity, and licensing constraints limit elasticity. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and the core occupation remains embodied and regulated, the net effect is resilient.

title: Dentists
rationale: Dentistry includes important cognitive tasks such as diagnosis from x-rays, treatment planning, documentation, patient communication, and practice administration, all of which AI can assist. However, the core work is still hands-on, licensed, high-liability care in a patient’s mouth requiring dexterity, anesthesia management, real-time judgment, and physical presence, so AI is unlikely to absorb most dentist tasks within 10 years. Demand has moderate elasticity because cost and access barriers suppress preventive, restorative, and cosmetic dental care, but total visits are constrained by insurance coverage, patient time, regulation, and finite biological need. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Desktop publishers
rationale: Desktop publishing is almost entirely digital work involving layout, formatting, image editing, proofreading, and file preparation, all of which are directly affected by generative design tools, automated templates, AI image editing, and document-layout software. AI can already automate much of the routine production work and will increasingly allow editors, marketers, authors, and graphic designers to generate acceptable layouts without a dedicated desktop publisher. Demand elasticity is limited because the volume of newspapers, books, brochures, and formal page-layout work is not likely to expand enough to offset large productivity gains, especially as publishing continues shifting to digital formats and adjacent workers absorb these tasks. With very high disruption and low-to-moderate demand expansion, the occupation is likely to see headcount contraction rather than broad augmentation.

title: Diagnostic medical sonographers
rationale: AI can materially assist sonographers with image-quality guidance, automated measurements, abnormality detection, workflow documentation, and preliminary summaries, but the core job still requires hands-on probe manipulation, patient positioning, bedside communication, and adaptation to varied anatomy and patient conditions. Robotics and AI-guided ultrasound may reduce skill barriers over time, but widespread full automation is limited by clinical accountability, real-time physical interaction, and the need to obtain diagnostically adequate images. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper and faster ultrasound could expand screening, outpatient imaging, point-of-care use, and access in underserved settings, though utilization remains constrained by medical necessity, reimbursement, and clinician ordering patterns. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the physical core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Diesel service technicians and mechanics
rationale: Diesel mechanics do use computerized diagnostics, technical manuals, work orders, and electronic control-system data, so AI can improve troubleshooting, fault-code interpretation, repair guidance, scheduling, and predictive maintenance. However, the core work remains hands-on: inspecting vehicles, removing and replacing heavy components, using tools, test-driving, and working in unpredictable shop or roadside conditions. Demand is relatively inelastic because maintenance needs are tied to the stock of diesel vehicles, freight activity, and regulatory/safety requirements; cheaper diagnosis may increase preventive maintenance somewhat, but fleets will not consume vastly more repairs just because they are faster. Because AI affects important diagnostic and administrative portions but does not reshape the physical core of the job, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Dietitians and nutritionists
rationale: Dietitians and nutritionists perform substantial cognitive and language-based work—assessing nutrition needs, interpreting labs and research, creating meal plans, counseling clients, producing educational materials, and documenting progress—all areas where AI can materially assist. Human licensure, clinical accountability, empathy, behavior-change coaching, and coordination with healthcare teams limit full replacement, especially for complex medical nutrition therapy. Demand elasticity is high because personalized nutrition advice is currently constrained by cost, access, and clinician availability, while obesity, diabetes, aging, sports nutrition, and preventive care create large latent demand. Because disruption is high but cheaper AI-enabled services are likely to expand the market for nutrition support, the occupation is best classified as augment.

title: Drafters
rationale: Drafting is predominantly digital technical work in CAD and BIM, involving the conversion of sketches, specifications, and design intent into detailed drawings, which is directly exposed to AI-assisted design, automated documentation, generative design, clash detection, and model-to-drawing tools. Human judgment, code knowledge, coordination with engineers and architects, and occasional site context remain important, but many routine drawing, detailing, dimensioning, and revision tasks are highly automatable. Demand for drafting output is constrained by the number of construction, engineering, and manufacturing projects, so making drafting much faster and cheaper would create some additional design iteration and documentation but not enough to expand projects proportionally. Because disruption is high and demand elasticity is low, productivity gains are likely to reduce the need for dedicated drafters, with more drafting absorbed by engineers, architects, and AI-enabled design software.

title: Drywall installers, ceiling tile installers, and tapers
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical: lifting, cutting, fastening, taping, sanding, and finishing materials in varied construction environments. AI may help with estimating, scheduling, measuring from plans, layout guidance, or quality inspection, and robotics may assist in limited standardized settings, but the occupation still requires dexterity, mobility, and on-site judgment. Demand is tied mainly to construction and remodeling activity, so cheaper drywall labor would create only limited additional demand because housing, commercial construction, permitting, financing, and materials are larger constraints. Because disruption is low and AI mostly affects peripheral tasks rather than the core trade, the occupation is resilient.

title: Economists
rationale: Economists perform predominantly digital, cognitive work: data collection and cleaning, statistical modeling, forecasting, literature review, report writing, and presentations. AI is already useful for coding, econometric workflows, summarizing research, generating charts, drafting reports, and exploring scenarios, though human judgment remains important for causal identification, institutional context, policy credibility, and advising decision makers. Demand could expand as cheaper analysis lets more firms, agencies, and nonprofits use economic modeling for pricing, regulation, labor markets, and forecasting, but growth is limited by government budgets, finite policy decisions, trust requirements, and the specialized nature of high-stakes economic advice. High disruption combined with moderate elasticity means the occupation is likely to be restructured rather than broadly replaced, with economists who use AI becoming much more productive while routine analyst tasks shrink.

title: Editors
rationale: Editing is almost entirely language-based digital work, and AI tools already perform proofreading, grammar correction, rewriting, headline generation, summarization, and first-pass style edits at high speed. Human editors remain important for judgment, taste, ethics, source credibility, publication strategy, and managing writers, but many routine copyediting and developmental editing tasks are directly exposed. Demand could expand as cheaper editing enables more self-published books, marketing content, newsletters, technical documentation, and AI-generated drafts to be polished, but traditional publishing and media budgets limit how much headcount can grow. Because disruption is very high while demand elasticity is only moderate, the occupation is likely to be restructured rather than simply augmented.

title: Electrical and electronic engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: This occupation has a substantial cognitive and digital component—reading schematics, analyzing test data, documenting results, troubleshooting designs, and using diagnostic software—where AI can materially improve productivity. However, much of the core work remains hands-on and site- or lab-based, including assembling prototypes, calibrating instruments, soldering components, replacing circuitry, and operating test equipment, which limits full AI substitution over the next decade. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper and faster testing and prototyping could support more electronics development, automation, and maintenance, but demand is constrained by manufacturing investment cycles, physical equipment, and relatively slow projected occupational growth. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to fully reshape or absorb the occupation’s physical core, the net effect is resilient.

title: Electrical and electronics engineers
rationale: Electrical and electronics engineering has a large digital and analytical component: requirements analysis, circuit and system design, CAD/EDA modeling, simulation, documentation, programming, and troubleshooting are all areas where AI tools can materially accelerate work. However, the occupation also depends on physical testing, lab work, safety validation, manufacturing constraints, field observation, regulatory accountability, and integration with real-world hardware, which limits full automation. Demand should expand meaningfully as cheaper engineering enables more electronics, grid modernization, electrification, communications systems, semiconductors, and product variants, but growth is constrained by capital costs, manufacturing capacity, certification cycles, and physical deployment. Because disruption is high but demand elasticity is only moderate, the occupation is best categorized as restructure: engineers will remain important, but workflows and required skills will shift substantially toward AI-assisted design, verification, integration, and oversight.

title: Electrical and electronics installers and repairers
rationale: AI will improve diagnostic work through smarter test equipment, fault-code interpretation, predictive maintenance systems, augmented-reality repair guidance, and automated recordkeeping. However, the core job still requires physical presence, hands-on inspection, disassembly, component replacement, safety judgment, and work in factories, vehicles, substations, and repair shops. Demand is only modestly elastic because maintenance needs are largely tied to the installed base of equipment, grid infrastructure, transportation systems, and replacement cycles, though cheaper diagnostics may support more preventive maintenance. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Electrical power-line installers and repairers
rationale: The core work is physical, hazardous, and site-specific: climbing poles or towers, operating bucket trucks, stringing cable, replacing transformers, and restoring service in storms. AI can materially improve peripheral and semi-core tasks such as outage prediction, dispatch, drone-based inspection, fault localization, safety monitoring, and training, but it is unlikely to automate most hands-on repair and installation work within 10 years. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper, faster work would support more grid hardening, EV-related connections, renewable integration, and maintenance, although utility regulation, capital budgets, permitting, and physical infrastructure constraints limit expansion. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite useful AI-enabled tools, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Electricians
rationale: Electricians’ core work is physical, site-specific, safety-critical, and licensed: installing wiring, troubleshooting live systems, working in walls, panels, factories, and construction sites. AI can help with peripheral and cognitive tasks such as code lookup, blueprint interpretation, estimating, scheduling, documentation, and diagnostic guidance, but it cannot perform most hands-on installation and repair work over the next decade. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper and faster electrical work would likely unlock more home upgrades, EV charger installations, solar and battery connections, smart-building retrofits, and deferred maintenance, though demand remains constrained by construction cycles, physical infrastructure, and regulation. Because disruption is low-to-moderate despite meaningful AI assistance at the margins, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Electro-mechanical and mechatronics technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can materially assist with reading schematics, troubleshooting faults, analyzing test data, generating maintenance reports, and using predictive diagnostics, so the knowledge-work portion of this occupation is meaningfully exposed. However, the core job still involves hands-on operation, calibration, soldering, measurement, repair, and onsite interaction with complex physical equipment, which limits full automation over the next decade. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper diagnostics and support could make robotic and automated systems easier to deploy and maintain, but demand is constrained by manufacturing investment cycles, physical equipment needs, and onsite service requirements. Because disruption is significant but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient rather than replaced or restructured.

title: Elementary, middle, and high school principals
rationale: AI can materially assist principals with administrative and analytical tasks such as scheduling, drafting reports, analyzing test-score data, budgeting, communications, and planning professional development. However, the core role still depends heavily on in-person leadership, student discipline, parent and teacher relationship management, safety decisions, crisis response, and legal accountability for a school community. Demand is highly inelastic because the number of principals is mostly tied to the number of schools, enrollment, and district budgets rather than the cost or speed of administrative work. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient even though AI will streamline many back-office tasks.

title: Elevator and escalator installers and repairers
rationale: The core work is physical, site-specific, safety-critical installation and repair involving heavy components, wiring, confined spaces, heights, and licensed hands-on judgment. AI can help with diagnostics, predictive maintenance, documentation, code lookup, service records, and interpreting manuals or blueprints, but it is unlikely to automate the main field tasks over the next decade. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of elevators and escalators is tied to building stock, construction, regulation, and required maintenance cycles, though cheaper diagnostics may modestly expand preventive service and modernization. Because disruption is low-to-moderate, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Emergency management directors
rationale: AI can materially assist emergency management directors with hazard analysis, scenario modeling, drafting emergency plans, grant applications, public communications, damage assessment synthesis, and real-time information monitoring. However, the core role depends heavily on accountable leadership, interagency coordination, public trust, field knowledge, and high-stakes decisions during unpredictable real-world crises, which keeps disruption below the high-disruption threshold. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper planning and analytics could let more small governments, hospitals, universities, and firms improve preparedness, but public budgets, jurisdictional structures, and the need for human authority limit headcount expansion. Because disruption is significant but not high enough to reshape or automate the core occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: EMTs and paramedics
rationale: EMTs and paramedics perform highly physical, unpredictable, in-person work: assessing patients at emergency scenes, lifting and transporting them, administering treatments, and coordinating with police, firefighters, hospitals, and families. AI can improve peripheral and cognitive components such as dispatch triage, documentation, protocol guidance, EKG interpretation, and real-time clinical decision support, but it cannot replace the need for trained responders physically present in chaotic environments. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of emergencies, transports, and age-related acute events is driven by population health and accidents rather than the price of EMT labor, though cheaper services could modestly expand community paramedicine or nonemergency response capacity. Because disruption is below the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Entertainment and recreation managers
rationale: AI can materially assist with scheduling, budgeting, marketing copy, customer feedback analysis, staff planning, and program design, but the core job still involves on-site operations, safety oversight, staff leadership, vendor coordination, and resolving participant issues in real time. Much of the value comes from human judgment, interpersonal presence, and accountability for physical facilities and experiences, limiting disruption to a moderate level. Demand could expand somewhat as cheaper planning tools enable more customized classes, events, and recreation programs, but growth is constrained by venues, staffing, safety requirements, and local participation. Because disruption is below the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Environmental engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: This occupation has a substantial physical and site-specific component: collecting air, soil, and water samples, operating pumps and instruments, handling hazardous materials, and inspecting facilities all require real-world presence and safety judgment. AI and automation can meaningfully improve the digital and analytical portions, including sensor monitoring, lab data interpretation, compliance documentation, scheduling, and report review, but they do not replace much of the field execution. Demand could expand moderately if monitoring and testing become cheaper, because more facilities, sites, and municipalities may conduct more frequent environmental assessment, though regulatory budgets and project pipelines limit unlimited growth. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with AI mostly augmenting productivity rather than reshaping the core role.

title: Environmental engineers
rationale: Environmental engineering includes substantial cognitive and digital work—data analysis, modeling, report drafting, permit preparation, compliance documentation, and design support—that AI can materially accelerate. However, the core occupation also depends on site-specific engineering judgment, field inspections, physical infrastructure, regulatory accountability, stakeholder coordination, and licensed sign-off, which limit full automation. Demand would expand moderately if engineering analysis became cheaper, especially for smaller firms, municipalities, remediation planning, and environmental monitoring, but total demand is constrained by regulation, public budgets, and the capital cost of physical projects. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the entire occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Environmental science and protection technicians
rationale: AI can materially improve the digital and analytical parts of this job, including interpreting sensor data, flagging anomalies, drafting compliance reports, managing sample records, and supporting environmental modeling. However, many core tasks still require field presence, site inspections, equipment setup, sample collection, chain-of-custody handling, laboratory procedures, and judgment in real-world conditions, which limits overall disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper monitoring and analysis could expand testing frequency, coverage of sites, and compliance services, but much of the work is still driven by regulation, budgets, and physical sampling needs. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Environmental scientists and specialists
rationale: AI can substantially assist environmental scientists with literature review, GIS and remote-sensing analysis, pollutant modeling, regulatory research, data interpretation, and drafting reports or presentations. However, the occupation still depends on site-specific judgment, field investigations, laboratory sampling workflows, stakeholder communication, and professional accountability for compliance and environmental risk recommendations. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis could expand monitoring, climate-risk assessment, compliance support, and consulting for smaller organizations, but much of the work is driven by regulation, public budgets, construction activity, and physical remediation needs. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to overtake the field-based and judgment-heavy core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Epidemiologists
rationale: Epidemiology is heavily cognitive and data-driven: statistical analysis, surveillance, literature review, study design, reporting, grant writing, and policy communication are all areas where AI can materially accelerate work. However, the occupation also requires human judgment about causal inference, public-health ethics, field realities, community trust, emergency coordination, and accountability to agencies and policymakers, so AI is unlikely to simply automate the role end-to-end. Demand should expand meaningfully because cheaper analysis can support more disease surveillance, hospital infection-control programs, outbreak preparedness, and local public-health analytics, but growth is limited by government budgets, regulation, and institutional adoption. The result is restructuring: epidemiologists will remain needed, but workflows and required skills will shift toward AI-assisted analytics, validation, interpretation, and public-health decision-making.

title: Exercise physiologists
rationale: AI can meaningfully assist exercise physiologists with documentation, interpreting wearable or test data, risk stratification, and generating individualized exercise plans. However, the core work still involves hands-on assessment, use of medical equipment, observing movement and exertion, motivating clients, and monitoring safety for people with chronic conditions, so AI is unlikely to absorb most daily tasks. Demand elasticity is relatively high because cheaper personalized exercise programming could expand use in chronic disease management, preventive health, aging populations, and remote coaching, though reimbursement and the need for human supervision limit full scaling. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation fits the resilient category despite meaningful AI-enabled productivity gains.

title: Farmers, ranchers, and other agricultural managers
rationale: AI will meaningfully affect the analytical and administrative parts of farm management, including yield forecasting, precision input use, market monitoring, compliance records, labor scheduling, and equipment diagnostics. However, the core occupation remains tied to land, animals, machinery, weather, facilities, and unpredictable on-site supervision, so AI changes many decisions but does not fully absorb the work. Demand for agricultural output is relatively inelastic and constrained by land, biology, water, regulation, and commodity markets, so cheaper management mainly supports consolidation and productivity rather than much more employment. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation fits the resilient category despite low demand elasticity.

title: Fashion designers
rationale: Fashion design includes substantial digital and cognitive work—trend research, concept generation, CAD sketching, color and pattern exploration, virtual fitting, and marketing—that generative AI can already accelerate meaningfully. Human designers still matter for taste, brand identity, fabric feel, fit, collaboration with manufacturers, and final creative judgment, but many core ideation and iteration tasks are directly in AI’s path. Demand could expand through faster trend cycles, lower-cost niche collections, personalization, and direct-to-consumer brands, but it is constrained by physical production, inventory risk, consumer apparel budgets, and sustainability concerns. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is likely to be restructured rather than broadly replaced or strongly augmented.

title: Film and video editors and camera operators
rationale: Disruption is high but uneven: film and video editing is almost entirely digital, and AI already helps with transcription, logging, rough cuts, color correction, audio cleanup, captions, and generative b-roll, while camera operation still requires physical presence, judgment, equipment handling, and real-time adaptation. Robotic cameras, drones, and generative video will further reduce some routine shooting and postproduction tasks, especially in corporate, social, and low-budget content. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper video production would unlock much more marketing, training, social media, localization, personalized advertising, and creator content, although attention limits and the need for real-world footage cap expansion somewhat. Because disruption is high but cheaper output is likely to generate substantially more video production, the occupation is best categorized as augment rather than replace.

title: Financial analysts
rationale: Financial analysts perform highly digital, cognitive work: evaluating financial statements, market data, economic trends, valuation models, risks, and writing recommendations, all of which are directly affected by AI tools. AI can already accelerate data ingestion, comparable-company analysis, scenario modeling, earnings-call summaries, report drafting, and portfolio/risk monitoring, though human judgment, accountability, client communication, and investment decision ownership remain important. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper analysis can expand coverage to more securities, private companies, small investors, and real-time risk use cases, but total demand is constrained by assets under management, regulatory requirements, trust, and the zero-sum nature of many investment decisions. The occupation is therefore likely to be restructured: fewer workers will be needed for routine modeling and reporting, while successful analysts will shift toward judgment, strategy, differentiated insight, client-facing explanation, and oversight of AI-driven workflows.

title: Financial clerks
rationale: Financial clerks perform highly routine, rules-based administrative work: updating records, calculating charges, processing applications, verifying transactions, preparing documents, and answering account questions. These tasks are largely digital and already being automated by online self-service portals, workflow software, OCR, RPA, credit-scoring systems, payroll platforms, and increasingly AI customer-service and document-processing tools. Demand is relatively inelastic because organizations do not need ten times as many payroll runs, invoices, account openings, loan files, or insurance policy changes simply because processing becomes cheaper; volumes are mostly driven by underlying business activity. Because AI can absorb much of the core work and productivity gains are likely to reduce staffing rather than unlock large new demand, this occupation fits the replace category.

title: Financial examiners
rationale: Financial examiners perform highly cognitive, document-heavy work: reviewing financial statements, loan files, meeting minutes, regulations, and drafting risk and compliance reports, all of which are directly affected by AI tools for analysis, anomaly detection, document review, and report generation. However, the role also requires supervisory judgment, legal accountability, institution-specific context, and sometimes onsite examination, so AI is more likely to transform workflows than fully eliminate the occupation. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper examination can enable more continuous monitoring, deeper reviews, and broader coverage of complex financial products, but the number of regulated institutions and formal examination requirements limit unlimited expansion. Because disruption is high while demand expansion is meaningful but not enough to fully absorb productivity gains, the occupation is best categorized as restructure.

title: Financial managers
rationale: Financial managers do predominantly cognitive, data-intensive work: forecasting, reporting, compliance monitoring, cost analysis, risk assessment, and advising executives, all of which AI can materially accelerate through automated modeling, anomaly detection, scenario analysis, and report generation. However, the role also includes supervision, judgment under uncertainty, regulatory accountability, and communication with senior leadership, so AI is more likely to change the workflow than fully replace the manager. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper financial analysis will let firms do more real-time planning, risk management, and strategic evaluation, especially in smaller organizations, but each organization has a limited need for accountable finance leadership. The occupation therefore fits 'restructure': AI will substantially reshape required skills and reduce some analyst/reporting labor, while increasing the premium on strategic judgment, governance, and AI-enabled decision-making.

title: Fire inspectors
rationale: Fire inspectors have substantial on-site, physical, and legal-enforcement components: walking buildings or outdoor areas, testing equipment, observing hazards, collecting evidence, interviewing witnesses, and sometimes exercising police powers. AI can materially assist with blueprint/code review, report drafting, photo or sensor analysis, wildfire-risk modeling, scheduling, and documentation, but it is unlikely to replace the need for credentialed human inspection and judgment in unpredictable real-world environments. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper inspection and risk-analysis tools could enable more frequent prevention work, especially for wildfire and older-building compliance, but demand is still constrained by construction activity, legal requirements, and public-sector budgets. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Firefighters
rationale: Firefighting is dominated by physical, hazardous, and highly unpredictable real-world tasks: entering burning structures, rescuing people, operating heavy equipment, providing emergency medical aid, and managing chaotic incident scenes. AI can improve dispatch, route optimization, fire prediction, drone-based situational awareness, incident reporting, training simulations, and equipment monitoring, but these tools mostly support rather than replace the core work. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of fires, medical emergencies, crashes, and disasters does not rise dramatically just because response labor becomes cheaper, and staffing is largely determined by public safety coverage needs and government budgets. Because disruption to the core occupation remains low-to-moderate, the appropriate net effect is resilient.

title: Fishing and hunting workers
rationale: The core work of fishing and hunting workers is physical, hazardous, and location-specific: operating vessels or traps, handling gear, sorting and storing catch, and working in unpredictable outdoor conditions. AI can improve peripheral or enabling tasks such as fish-location prediction, navigation, weather risk assessment, equipment monitoring, and regulatory recordkeeping, but it does not replace most hands-on labor over the next decade. Demand is highly inelastic because catch volumes are constrained by fish stocks, seasons, quotas, permits, and wildlife regulations, so cheaper search or operations would not translate into proportionally more legal output. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite low elasticity, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Fitness trainers and instructors
rationale: AI can meaningfully assist with workout programming, nutrition guidance, progress tracking, scheduling, marketing, and even video-based form feedback, but the core job still depends heavily on in-person demonstration, motivation, safety monitoring, and relationship-building. Many clients value accountability, social interaction, and real-time human judgment in a gym, class, or home setting, which limits full automation over the next decade. Demand elasticity is fairly high because lower-cost personalized coaching and hybrid digital support could expand access to people who cannot afford frequent one-on-one training today. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite meaningful AI-enabled changes at the margins.

title: Flight attendants
rationale: Flight attendants’ core work requires physical presence in an aircraft cabin: enforcing safety rules, monitoring passengers, assisting with boarding and emergencies, providing first aid, and managing disruptive behavior. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as announcements, translation, passenger information, incident reports, scheduling, and inventory, but it cannot practically or legally substitute for certified onboard safety personnel over the next decade. Demand elasticity is low because staffing is tied to FAA requirements, aircraft size, and flight volumes rather than the speed of individual tasks; cheaper AI-assisted service would not cause airlines to use dramatically more flight attendants. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and the core occupation remains anchored in regulated, in-person safety work, the net effect is resilient.

title: Flooring installers and tile and stone setters
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical, on-site, and variable: removing old materials, preparing uneven surfaces, cutting and fitting flooring, spreading mortar or adhesives, setting tile or carpet, grouting, sanding, and finishing. AI may help with estimates, measurements, design visualization, scheduling, quoting, and material optimization, but it does not meaningfully replace the dexterous manual work in unpredictable homes and commercial spaces over the next decade. Demand has some price sensitivity because cheaper installation could encourage more renovations or higher-end flooring choices, but it is constrained by housing turnover, construction activity, materials costs, and the finite number of floors and surfaces needing replacement. Because disruption is low and AI mainly affects peripheral planning and administrative tasks, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Floral designers
rationale: Floral design includes some AI-exposed tasks such as taking orders, recommending flower combinations, generating visual concepts, pricing, marketing, and managing inventory. However, the core work remains hands-on: selecting perishable materials, cutting and arranging flowers, maintaining freshness, interacting with local customers, and setting up displays at events. Demand would expand only modestly if design labor became cheaper because purchases are tied to occasions, input costs, delivery logistics, and the number of weddings, funerals, holidays, and commercial accounts. Because AI affects peripheral and planning tasks more than the physical craft itself, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Food and beverage serving and related workers
rationale: AI and related automation can materially affect order-taking, payment, reservations, drive-thru interactions, scheduling, and some customer questions through kiosks, apps, and voice systems. However, much of the occupation still involves physical presence: preparing simple items, carrying food, clearing tables, stocking stations, cleaning areas, and handling unpredictable customer-service situations. Demand for restaurant and prepared-food service would expand somewhat if service labor became cheaper, but it is constrained by food costs, real estate, meal frequency, and consumers’ limited appetite for eating out. Because the core work remains substantially physical and on-site, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite partial task automation.

title: Food preparation workers
rationale: The core tasks of food preparation workers are physical, hands-on activities such as chopping, cleaning, stocking, measuring, moving supplies, and maintaining sanitation in fast-paced kitchens. AI may improve scheduling, inventory, ordering, temperature monitoring, and eventually support some robotic prep in standardized settings, but most daily work requires dexterity, mobility, and adaptation to a real kitchen environment. Demand elasticity is limited because people do not eat vastly more meals if prep labor gets cheaper, although lower-cost prepared foods and restaurant meals could modestly expand demand. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate and AI mostly affects peripheral or highly standardized tasks, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Food processing equipment workers
rationale: Core work is tied to operating, loading, cleaning, and physically monitoring food-processing machinery in regulated production environments, so AI cannot directly perform much of the hands-on work without broader robotics and plant automation. AI-enabled sensors, computer vision quality checks, predictive maintenance, and recipe/process optimization can change monitoring and adjustment tasks, but these are complements to equipment operation rather than full substitutes for most workers over the next decade. Demand for processed food is relatively inelastic because people do not consume vastly more food when production labor becomes cheaper, though convenience foods and product variety create some limited expansion. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate, the occupation is best categorized as resilient despite some ongoing automation pressure.

title: Food service managers
rationale: AI can materially improve parts of food service management such as scheduling, inventory ordering, payroll, demand forecasting, pricing, promotions, and compliance documentation. However, the core job still requires on-site supervision, real-time coordination of kitchen and dining room staff, handling customer complaints, inspecting facilities, and responding to unpredictable operational problems. Demand for managers would not expand dramatically if these tasks became cheaper, because restaurant demand is constrained by consumer dining habits, locations, labor availability, and margins, though some establishments may operate with leaner management. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Forensic science technicians
rationale: AI can materially assist forensic science technicians with DNA interpretation, image and pattern matching, database searches, statistical analysis, documentation, and technical report drafting. However, much of the occupation still depends on physical evidence collection, chain-of-custody procedures, laboratory handling, equipment operation, scene judgment, and courtroom testimony, all of which require validated human presence and accountability. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper analysis could reduce backlogs, expand testing of more evidence, and support more cold-case work, but caseloads, government budgets, court processes, and evidentiary standards limit explosive growth. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the entire core of the job, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Forest and conservation workers
rationale: Most core tasks are outdoor, physical, and variable: planting seedlings, clearing brush, cutting trees, maintaining trails, operating equipment, and helping with fire suppression. AI, drones, remote sensing, and computer vision can reduce some measurement, inventory, disease detection, and planning work, but they do not replace the hands-on field labor or emergency presence that defines the occupation. Demand could expand moderately if technology lowers costs, because wildfire mitigation, reforestation, and conservation needs are substantial, but government budgets, land-management constraints, and the physical nature of the work limit expansion. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite some automation pressure, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Fundraisers
rationale: Fundraising has many AI-exposed tasks: donor prospect research, segmentation, personalized email and social media outreach, campaign copywriting, CRM recordkeeping, compliance support, and performance analytics. However, the highest-value work still depends on trust, judgment, in-person relationship building, volunteer coordination, and event execution, so AI changes the workflow more than it fully replaces the role. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper fundraising tools will let smaller nonprofits and campaigns do more outreach, but total donor dollars and donor attention are limited and partly zero-sum across organizations. With high disruption but only moderate demand expansion, the occupation is likely to be restructured around AI-enabled donor strategy and relationship management rather than simply growing or disappearing.

title: Funeral service workers
rationale: AI can meaningfully assist with administrative and language-heavy tasks such as drafting obituaries, preparing forms, scheduling services, explaining options, marketing, and handling benefits or insurance paperwork. However, the occupation’s core still depends on in-person grief support, culturally sensitive judgment, licensed handling and preparation of remains, transportation, service coordination, and trust-based family interaction. Demand is highly tied to mortality and family customs, so making planning cheaper or faster would not create many more funerals, though it may increase preplanning and personalization somewhat. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite low demand elasticity, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Gambling services workers
rationale: Most gambling services work is in-person, customer-facing, and operational: dealing cards, monitoring tables, explaining rules, handling disputes, and maintaining the casino experience. AI and automation can affect parts of the job, especially sportsbook ticketing, fraud detection, surveillance, scheduling, customer service, and online gambling interfaces, but the core casino-floor role still depends heavily on human presence and hospitality. Demand elasticity is low because gambling demand is constrained by regulation, location, licensing, consumer budgets, and social limits; cheaper labor does not lead people to gamble 10 times more. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient, even though some subroles such as sportsbook writers and runners may face more automation pressure.

title: General maintenance and repair workers
rationale: General maintenance and repair work is dominated by hands-on physical tasks in varied real-world settings: inspecting equipment, using tools, replacing parts, painting, repairing flooring, and working around buildings and machinery. AI can help with troubleshooting guides, work-order triage, predictive maintenance alerts, supply ordering, estimating, documentation, and training, but it does not perform the core manual repair work without capable general-purpose robotics. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper, faster maintenance would unlock some deferred repairs and more preventive upkeep, especially in aging buildings, but the need is still bounded by the stock of buildings and equipment. Because disruption to the core occupation remains low-to-moderate, the net effect is resilient.

title: General office clerks
rationale: General office clerks perform many routine digital and language-based tasks—answering calls, scheduling, typing and formatting documents, filing records, processing forms, and entering data—that are directly targeted by AI, workflow software, automated phone systems, and document management tools. Some duties still involve physical office presence, mail handling, visitors, and local coordination, but these are a minority of the core task bundle in many settings. Demand elasticity is low because organizations do not need dramatically more filing, data entry, scheduling, or routine document processing simply because it becomes cheaper; productivity gains mostly reduce the number of clerks needed. Therefore the occupation fits the replace category: disruption is high and demand expansion is too limited to offset automation-driven headcount pressure.

title: Genetic counselors
rationale: Genetic counseling is heavily cognitive and language-based: collecting histories, interpreting genetic test results, explaining risks, documenting sessions, and researching new findings are all areas where AI can substantially assist. However, the role also involves licensed clinical judgment, informed consent, coordination with physicians, and emotionally sensitive counseling, which limits full automation. Demand is fairly elastic because genetic testing and genomic medicine are expanding, and access to counseling is currently constrained by cost, availability, and specialist shortages. Because AI is likely to let counselors handle more cases and support broader use of genetic testing rather than simply eliminate the human role, the net effect is augment.

title: Geographers
rationale: Geographers perform a large share of digital and analytical work: GIS analysis, remote sensing interpretation, map production, data linkage, visualization, and report writing are all areas where AI and automated geospatial tools are already becoming materially useful. Some tasks still require human fieldwork, interviews, project framing, and interdisciplinary judgment, which keeps disruption below the most exposed fully digital occupations. Demand for geographic analysis may grow somewhat with climate risk, infrastructure planning, disaster response, and location intelligence, but employment is small and heavily tied to government funding and fixed planning budgets, limiting expansion. With high disruption and relatively low elasticity, AI is likely to reduce the number of workers needed for routine mapping, analysis, and reporting even as remaining geographers shift toward higher-level interpretation and advisory roles.

title: Geological and hydrologic technicians
rationale: This occupation has a substantial AI-exposed component: organizing sensor and lab data, GIS mapping, report drafting, database compilation, and interpreting routine geological or hydrologic measurements can be accelerated by AI, drones, remote sensing, and automated analytics. However, many core tasks still require physical presence in the field or lab, including collecting samples, installing and maintaining equipment, handling instruments, and working in remote or variable conditions. Demand could expand moderately if monitoring, mapping, and analysis become cheaper, especially for water management, environmental compliance, and resource exploration, but it is constrained by project funding, regulation, commodity cycles, and the need for physical sampling. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the entire occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Geoscientists
rationale: Geoscientists do substantial digital and cognitive work—GIS analysis, remote sensing interpretation, modeling, lab-data analysis, mapping, reporting, and presentations—that AI can materially accelerate. However, the occupation also depends heavily on fieldwork, sample collection, site-specific observation, laboratory procedures, professional judgment, and often licensure, which limits full automation of the core role. Demand could expand moderately as cheaper analysis enables more environmental monitoring, hazard assessment, resource evaluation, and renewable-energy siting, but it remains constrained by physical projects, regulation, budgets, and field access. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Glaziers
rationale: Glaziers’ core work is physical, site-specific installation: measuring openings, lifting and positioning heavy glass, fastening frames, sealing joints, and working safely at heights or in variable construction environments. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as blueprint interpretation, estimating, scheduling, digital measurement, fabrication planning, and quality checks, but it does not directly replace the manual jobsite execution. Demand is somewhat price-sensitive because cheaper installation could encourage more window replacement, energy-efficiency retrofits, and architectural glass use, but it remains constrained by construction cycles, material costs, building codes, and the pace of renovation. Because disruption is low and the core occupation remains hands-on, the net effect is resilient.

title: Graphic designers
rationale: Graphic design is almost entirely digital creative work involving layout, image generation, typography, editing, and client revisions, all of which are directly affected by generative AI and automated design tools. AI can already produce drafts, variations, logos, ads, social media graphics, and production-ready assets, shifting designers toward art direction, brand strategy, taste-making, prompt workflows, and client interpretation. Demand will expand somewhat because cheaper design enables more small businesses, creators, and marketing teams to produce more visual content, but much routine work will also be self-served by non-designers. Because disruption is very high but elasticity is only moderate, the occupation is best classified as restructure rather than full augmentation or replacement.

title: Grounds maintenance workers
rationale: Grounds maintenance is overwhelmingly hands-on, outdoor, and site-specific work involving mowing, planting, trimming, lifting, chemical application, tree work, and equipment operation in variable physical environments. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as scheduling, routing, customer communication, plant-health diagnostics, drone inspection, and some robotic mowing, but most core tasks still require human dexterity, judgment, and physical presence. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper service could lead homeowners, campuses, municipalities, and commercial properties to buy more frequent or higher-quality landscaping, but total land area, seasonality, and maintenance needs limit expansion. Because disruption to the core occupation remains low, the net effect is resilient.

title: Hand laborers and material movers
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical: lifting, carrying, packing, stocking shelves, cleaning vehicles, feeding machines, and collecting refuse in varied real-world environments. AI-enabled warehouse robots, routing software, vision systems, conveyors, and automated sorting will reduce some picking, packing, and machine-feeding tasks, but broad replacement is limited by low wages, messy environments, and the need for flexible human handling. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because cheaper material handling can support more e-commerce and faster fulfillment, but the underlying quantity of goods, trash, vehicles, and store inventory is not likely to expand dramatically just because labor is cheaper. Because disruption remains below the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with automation pressure concentrated in specific subgroups rather than a wholesale AI reshaping of the occupation.

title: Hazardous materials removal workers
rationale: The core work is physical, site-specific, hazardous, and often done in unpredictable environments such as old buildings, disaster sites, confined spaces, or decommissioned facilities. AI can help with monitoring, material identification, compliance documentation, training, scheduling, and possibly drone or robotic inspection, but it does not replace most hands-on removal, containment, packaging, transport, and equipment operation over the next decade. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper and safer cleanup could unlock more remediation of contaminated sites and older buildings, but activity is still constrained by regulation, public funding, construction cycles, and the finite number of hazardous sites. Because disruption to the core occupation remains low-to-moderate, the net effect is resilient.

title: Health and safety engineers
rationale: Health and safety engineers have substantial cognitive and document-heavy work that AI can assist with, including interpreting regulations, reviewing plans, drafting safety programs, analyzing incident data, and preparing reports. However, much of the core role still depends on site inspections, contextual engineering judgment, worker interviews, accountability, and understanding physical processes in real environments, which keeps disruption below the high-disruption threshold. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper safety analysis could enable more frequent audits, better monitoring, and expanded service to smaller firms, but demand remains constrained by regulation, facility count, capital projects, and compliance cycles. Because AI will reshape many analytical and administrative components but not absorb the occupation’s physical, judgment-based, and accountable core, the net effect is resilient.

title: Health education specialists
rationale: Health education specialists do substantial language- and knowledge-based work: creating educational materials, designing programs, analyzing community health data, writing grants, evaluating outcomes, and training others, all of which AI can materially accelerate. However, the occupation also depends on human trust, facilitation, cultural competence, community presence, advocacy, and coordination with healthcare and public agencies, so AI is unlikely to fully replace the role. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper personalized health education and prevention could expand access, especially for chronic disease management and underserved communities, but budgets, reimbursement rules, public funding cycles, and the need for in-person engagement limit explosive growth. The result is restructuring: fewer workers may be needed for routine content and analysis, while successful specialists will focus more on program strategy, relationship-building, implementation, and oversight of AI-enabled education tools.

title: Health information technologists and medical registrars
rationale: This occupation is heavily digital and data-oriented: workers abstract clinical records, maintain registries, validate data, generate reports, support health information systems, and ensure compliance. AI and NLP tools can increasingly extract information from medical records, assign codes, flag data-quality issues, draft reports, and support analytics, although human oversight remains important because of clinical nuance, privacy rules, and institutional workflows. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper health-data work would enable more quality measurement, registry expansion, population-health analytics, and compliance monitoring, but demand is still constrained by regulation, healthcare budgets, and fixed reporting requirements. The result is best categorized as restructure: routine abstraction and reporting will be automated, while demand shifts toward AI-supervised data governance, system implementation, validation, compliance, and higher-level analytics.

title: Heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers
rationale: HVAC work is dominated by hands-on installation, repair, testing, lifting, wiring, refrigerant handling, and troubleshooting in varied homes and buildings, so AI cannot directly perform most core tasks without advanced robotics and physical presence. AI can still help with diagnostics, predictive maintenance, load calculations, scheduling, customer communication, parts identification, and guided repair workflows, but these are mostly assistive rather than substitutive. Demand has moderate elasticity: cheaper service could increase preventive maintenance, retrofits, heat-pump conversions, and energy-efficiency upgrades, but the number of buildings and HVAC systems limits unlimited expansion. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate and the physical core of the occupation is durable, the net effect is resilient.

title: Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers
rationale: The core task is real-world vehicle operation, which is harder than purely digital work, but long-haul highway driving is one of the physical occupations most directly targeted by AI and autonomous-vehicle systems. AI can already improve routing, compliance logs, safety monitoring, and dispatch, and over the next decade hub-to-hub autonomous trucking could automate a substantial share of interstate driving while leaving loading, inspections, edge cases, and local delivery to humans. Demand for freight transportation would rise somewhat if driver labor costs fell, but trucking demand is ultimately tied to goods consumption and supply chains, so it would not expand enough to absorb a large productivity shock. Because disruption is high and elasticity is low, the likely net effect is replacement, especially for routine long-haul roles.

title: Heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians
rationale: The occupation is dominated by hands-on inspection, disassembly, repair, replacement, welding, lifting, field travel, and work in unpredictable physical environments, which current AI cannot directly perform. AI will meaningfully assist with diagnostic software, service manuals, predictive maintenance alerts, parts identification, and guided troubleshooting, but these are complements to the technician’s physical and mechanical work rather than substitutes for the core job. Demand is relatively inelastic because the amount of repair work is mainly tied to the stock and utilization of heavy equipment, construction activity, farming, rail fleets, and maintenance cycles; cheaper diagnostics may increase preventive maintenance somewhat but will not create many times more equipment needing service. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and the core work remains embodied and site-specific, the net effect is resilient.

title: High school teachers
rationale: High school teaching includes many cognitive and language-based tasks that AI can materially change, such as lesson planning, grading, quiz generation, differentiated materials, parent communication, and individualized tutoring support. However, the occupation also has durable in-person functions: classroom management, motivation, supervision, social development, safeguarding, and compliance with school policies. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper instructional support could expand personalized help, electives, remediation, and feedback, but total demand is constrained by school-age population, public budgets, certification rules, and compulsory schooling structures. The result is restructuring rather than broad replacement: teachers remain necessary, but their role shifts toward orchestration, mentoring, assessment oversight, and managing AI-supported learning environments.

title: Historians
rationale: Historians perform heavily language- and knowledge-based work: gathering documents, reading sources, translating, summarizing, analyzing, and writing reports, articles, exhibits, and books. AI tools can already accelerate archival search, OCR, transcription, translation, literature review, drafting, and synthesis, although human expertise remains important for source criticism, interpretation, fieldwork, artifacts, and public engagement. Demand is relatively inelastic because many historian jobs depend on government, museum, nonprofit, or grant funding rather than market demand, and cheaper historical research is unlikely to create enough new funded positions. With high disruption and limited demand expansion, AI is likely to reduce the amount of historian labor needed for many research and writing tasks, fitting the replace category.

title: Home health and personal care aides
rationale: Most core tasks for home health and personal care aides are hands-on, in-person, and relational: bathing, dressing, lifting, cooking, cleaning, transportation, observation, and companionship. AI can help with scheduling, documentation, medication reminders, remote monitoring, care-plan prompts, and fall-risk alerts, but affordable robots are unlikely to replace the unpredictable physical and emotional work in clients’ homes within 10 years. Demand is highly elastic because elder care and disability support are strongly constrained by cost, family availability, and caregiver shortages, and cheaper support would likely increase hours of care and allow more people to remain at home. Because disruption to the core occupation is low-to-moderate despite strong demand growth, the net effect is resilient.

title: Human resources managers
rationale: Human resources managers do substantial cognitive, language-based, and administrative work that AI can affect directly, including drafting policies, screening recruiting funnels, analyzing workforce data, answering routine employee questions, preparing compliance materials, and supporting performance or compensation processes. However, the occupation also depends heavily on judgment, trust, conflict mediation, organizational politics, legal accountability, and leadership, which limits full automation of the managerial core. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper HR capabilities could expand access for smaller firms and enable more employee analytics, compliance monitoring, training, and engagement work, but total demand remains constrained by organization size and workforce headcount. The result is restructure: AI will substantially change HR managers’ tools and skill requirements, but the role is more likely to shift toward strategic advisory, employee relations, and AI-enabled oversight than disappear outright.

title: Human resources specialists
rationale: Human resources specialists perform many language- and data-heavy tasks, including screening resumes, drafting job postings, scheduling interviews, answering policy questions, maintaining records, and processing onboarding or benefits paperwork, all of which are directly exposed to AI and HR automation. Human judgment, interpersonal trust, compliance responsibility, and sensitive employee-relations work keep the occupation from being fully automatable, but the daily workflow is likely to change substantially. Demand elasticity is low because HR workload is largely tied to firm size, hiring volume, compliance requirements, and employee headcount; cheaper HR services may improve service quality or help small firms, but organizations will not consume 10 times as much HR labor. With high disruption and limited demand expansion, AI is likely to absorb a significant share of administrative and recruiting work, producing net headcount pressure even as remaining roles become more strategic and relationship-focused.

title: Hydrologists
rationale: Hydrologists do have fieldwork and sampling duties, but much of the occupation’s value comes from data analysis, forecasting, GIS/remote-sensing interpretation, modeling, report writing, and communicating technical findings—areas where AI and machine learning tools are already materially useful. AI can accelerate model calibration, anomaly detection, flood and drought forecasting, pollution-plume analysis, and report drafting, but human expertise remains important for field validation, regulatory credibility, project judgment, and stakeholder coordination. Demand could expand somewhat because cheaper hydrologic analysis would help more communities, developers, utilities, and agencies assess flood risk, drought, water quality, and infrastructure resilience, but hiring is constrained by public budgets, permitting cycles, and the finite number of water-related projects. The result is restructuring rather than outright replacement: fewer routine analysis tasks, more emphasis on AI-enabled modeling, field interpretation, interdisciplinary judgment, and decision support.

title: Industrial designers
rationale: Industrial design has a large digital and cognitive component: ideation, sketching, rendering, CAD modeling, user research synthesis, and presentation materials are all areas where generative AI and design automation can materially accelerate work. However, the occupation remains tied to physical products, manufacturing constraints, materials, safety, ergonomics, prototyping, and client collaboration, so AI is unlikely to fully absorb the role. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper design could enable more product variants, faster iteration, and access for smaller firms, but total demand is constrained by tooling costs, manufacturing economics, regulation, and consumer market limits. The occupation is therefore likely to be restructured rather than replaced, with designers shifting toward AI-assisted concept generation, evaluation, prototyping strategy, and cross-functional product judgment.

title: Industrial engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can materially assist the analytical and digital parts of this job, including statistical production studies, cost analysis, workflow diagrams, CAD/CAM-related documentation, scheduling analysis, and generating improvement recommendations from sensor or ERP data. However, much of the core work still depends on plant-floor observation, measuring real processes, understanding equipment constraints, coordinating with operators and engineers, and validating changes in a physical manufacturing environment. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper process-improvement analysis would encourage more continuous improvement and automation projects, especially among smaller manufacturers, but demand is constrained by the number of facilities, capital budgets, and implementation capacity. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to displace the occupation’s hands-on and site-specific core, the net effect is resilient.

title: Industrial engineers
rationale: Industrial engineering is heavily analytical and systems-oriented: data analysis, process modeling, simulation, optimization, documentation, and presentation of recommendations are all directly enhanced by AI. However, the occupation also requires on-site observation, collaboration with production workers and managers, safety judgment, and implementation in physical facilities, which limits full automation. Demand should expand because cheaper optimization would let more firms, hospitals, warehouses, and manufacturers continuously improve operations, but adoption is constrained by capital budgets, physical systems, and organizational change capacity. Because disruption is high but demand elasticity is only moderate, the occupation is likely to be restructured rather than broadly replaced or simply augmented.

title: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers, and millwrights
rationale: AI will materially improve diagnostic, predictive maintenance, scheduling, parts identification, and access to technical manuals, especially as industrial equipment becomes more sensor-rich and computerized. However, the core work remains hands-on, site-specific, and safety-critical: disassembling machinery, replacing components, aligning equipment, welding, lubricating, moving heavy machines, and verifying operation in real industrial environments. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper, faster maintenance can enable more preventive work, higher uptime, and broader adoption of automated machinery, but it is still constrained by the installed base of equipment and physical repair needs. Because disruption is only moderate and the physical core of the occupation remains difficult for AI to replace, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Industrial production managers
rationale: AI will substantially affect the analytical and coordination parts of industrial production management, including production scheduling, capacity planning, quality analytics, predictive maintenance, budgeting, and report generation. However, the role still depends heavily on onsite judgment, worker supervision, safety accountability, cross-functional leadership, and resolving unpredictable plant-floor problems, which keeps disruption below the high-disruption threshold. Demand elasticity is limited because the number of production managers is tied to plants, shifts, capital equipment, and manufacturing output rather than to a large pool of unmet demand for management services. The occupation is therefore best classified as resilient: AI will improve tools and decision support, but it is unlikely to replace the core managerial presence over the next decade.

title: Information clerks
rationale: Information clerks perform highly routine data, records, form-processing, scheduling, correspondence, and customer-information tasks that are directly exposed to AI chatbots, document automation, OCR, workflow software, and self-service portals. Some roles still require human presence, judgment, confidentiality, or physical handling, such as hotel front desks, court offices, licensing counters, and baggage or ticketing situations, but much of the core work is digital and rules-based. Demand is fairly inelastic because organizations do not need ten times more check-ins, applications, permits, orders, or records processing simply because clerical work becomes cheaper. With high disruption and limited demand expansion, productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount substantially, even though some public-facing and exception-handling roles remain.

title: Information security analysts
rationale: Information security analysis is predominantly digital, analytical work, and AI can already assist substantially with alert triage, threat intelligence, vulnerability discovery, log analysis, report drafting, and security configuration review. However, the work also involves adversarial judgment, organizational risk tradeoffs, incident coordination, compliance, and communication with technical and nontechnical stakeholders, so AI is more likely to reshape workflows than fully automate the role. Demand elasticity is high because cybersecurity needs are expanding rapidly due to cloud adoption, AI-enabled attacks, e-commerce, regulation, and many underserved small and mid-sized organizations that cannot currently afford strong security coverage. Because disruption is high but cheaper security capability is likely to unlock much broader protection and monitoring rather than simply reduce headcount, the net effect is augment.

title: Instructional coordinators
rationale: Instructional coordinators do substantial cognitive and language-based work: designing curricula, analyzing student data, reviewing materials, writing implementation procedures, and developing teacher training, all of which AI can materially accelerate. However, the role also depends on human judgment, school politics, classroom observation, trust-building with teachers, and implementation leadership, so AI is unlikely to fully absorb the job. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper curriculum design and data analysis could enable more customized materials, faster standards alignment, and more teacher support, but public-school budgets, regulation, and staffing structures limit expansion. The occupation therefore fits restructure: AI will significantly change the workflow and required skills, but not eliminate the need for human instructional leaders.

title: Insulation workers
rationale: Insulation work is overwhelmingly physical and site-specific: workers remove old materials, measure and cut insulation, spray foam, fasten materials, work in confined spaces, and handle safety hazards. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as estimating quantities from blueprints, scheduling jobs, documenting compliance, or optimizing energy-retrofit recommendations, but it does not substantially automate the core installation work over the next decade. Demand could expand moderately if lower labor costs make more retrofits and energy-efficiency upgrades economical, but it remains constrained by construction cycles, building access, materials costs, and the finite stock of buildings needing work. Because disruption is low, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Insurance sales agents
rationale: Insurance sales agents perform many language- and information-processing tasks that AI can materially affect: lead outreach, needs intake, quote comparison, policy explanation, renewal reminders, CRM updates, and basic claims guidance. Human trust, licensing, persuasion, and complex advisory situations still matter, especially for commercial, life, and financial-product-linked sales, but a large share of routine personal-lines and renewal work can shift to AI-assisted or direct online channels. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because insurance purchases are tied to assets, legal requirements, household risk needs, and premiums rather than the cost of agent labor; cheaper sales support may reduce underinsurance and improve cross-selling, but it will not create proportionally more policies.
