Because disruption is high and demand expansion is limited, the occupation is likely to see significant restructuring and headcount pressure, especially among routine captive or transactional agents.

title: Insurance underwriters
rationale: Insurance underwriting is predominantly digital, rules-based, and analytical: workers review applications, risk factors, third-party data, software recommendations, and pricing decisions. Automated underwriting is already central to the occupation, and modern AI can further handle document extraction, risk scoring, anomaly detection, policy comparison, and routine approval or rejection decisions, leaving humans mainly for exceptions and complex commercial cases. Demand elasticity is low because the number of people, vehicles, homes, businesses, and risks needing insurance does not expand dramatically just because underwriting becomes cheaper or faster, and demand is also constrained by regulation and insurer risk appetite. Because disruption is high and demand expansion is limited, AI is likely to reduce headcount while concentrating remaining jobs in oversight, complex-risk judgment, and compliance.

title: Interior designers
rationale: Interior design includes many AI-exposed tasks: generating concepts, mood boards, layouts, renderings, material palettes, cost estimates, and CAD/BIM-supported documentation. However, the occupation also depends on client interaction, site measurement, code and accessibility judgment, contractor coordination, procurement, and resolving real-world installation constraints, which limits full automation. Demand could expand as cheaper design tools make professional-looking design accessible to more homeowners, small businesses, and retailers, but overall demand is constrained by renovation budgets, construction timelines, and the cost of physical materials and labor. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is likely to be restructured rather than broadly replaced or purely augmented.

title: Interpreters and translators
rationale: The core work of converting spoken, signed, or written language is directly in the path of modern AI translation, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and localization tools, especially for written translation and routine interpreting. Human expertise remains important for high-stakes medical, legal, diplomatic, literary, cultural, and sign-language contexts where accuracy, trust, nuance, ethics, and interpersonal judgment matter. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper translation would enable more websites, documents, media, meetings, and services to be multilingual, but regulatory requirements, certification, liability, and the limited need for human involvement in routine cases constrain headcount growth. The occupation is therefore likely to be substantially restructured toward AI-assisted post-editing, quality assurance, specialized interpreting, and culturally sensitive or high-risk work rather than simply expanded or fully replaced.

title: Ironworkers
rationale: Ironworking is overwhelmingly physical, site-specific work involving positioning, aligning, bolting, welding, tying rebar, signaling cranes, and operating safely at heights or in changing outdoor conditions. AI may help with blueprint interpretation, project coordination, safety monitoring, layout, prefabrication planning, and equipment guidance, but it does not directly replace the core hands-on installation tasks over the next decade. Demand would expand somewhat if work became cheaper and faster, especially for infrastructure repair and commercial construction, but total construction activity is constrained by financing, permitting, land use, materials, and public budgets. Because disruption to the core occupation is low, the net effect is resilient.

title: Janitors and building cleaners
rationale: Janitorial work is predominantly physical, site-specific, and requires navigating varied real-world environments, handling trash, restrooms, spills, supplies, minor repairs, and security tasks. AI-enabled equipment such as autonomous floor scrubbers, robotic vacuums, sensors, and scheduling tools can reduce some routine cleaning time, especially in large predictable facilities, but they do not replace the broad hands-on role over the next decade. Demand is relatively inelastic because cleaning needs are tied to building square footage, occupancy, sanitation standards, and budgets; cheaper cleaning may increase frequency somewhat but is unlikely to create many times more work. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers
rationale: AI can materially affect parts of this occupation such as jewelry design, CAD modeling, appraisal document drafting, market-price research, gemstone imaging, and customer-facing sales support. However, much of the core work still involves fine manual manipulation, repair, polishing, soldering, stone setting, and trusted handling of valuable physical goods, so AI does not fully absorb the occupation. Demand elasticity is limited because jewelry demand is constrained by consumer budgets, fashion cycles, precious-material costs, and imports, although cheaper custom design and repair could unlock some additional demand. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation fits the resilient category despite ongoing productivity pressure from automation.

title: Judges and hearing officers
rationale: Judges and hearing officers perform highly language- and cognition-intensive work: reading briefs, researching law, summarizing records, applying precedent, and drafting opinions are all areas where AI can materially accelerate the workflow. However, the formal authority to preside, ensure due process, assess credibility, and issue binding decisions will remain human-controlled for legal legitimacy and accountability. Demand elasticity is low because the number of judges and hearing officers is largely determined by statutes, public budgets, court structures, and caseloads rather than by market price, though faster processing could reduce backlogs. With high disruption but limited demand expansion, productivity gains are more likely to reduce required headcount or slow hiring than to create many new positions.

title: Kindergarten and elementary school teachers
rationale: AI can materially change lesson planning, worksheet generation, grading support, progress monitoring, parent communication, and individualized practice, so a significant share of teachers' cognitive and administrative work is exposed. However, the core job in kindergarten and elementary grades still requires in-person classroom management, child supervision, social-emotional development, motivation, safety, and adapting to unpredictable young children. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper AI-enabled instruction could expand tutoring, enrichment, and personalization, but public school staffing is constrained by enrollment, budgets, regulation, and the need for adult supervision. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to displace the in-person core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Labor relations specialists
rationale: Labor relations specialists perform heavily language- and document-based knowledge work, including drafting agreements and policies, interpreting contract terms, preparing grievance materials, compliance tracking, and training content, all of which AI can materially accelerate. However, the most sensitive parts of the job—negotiation, mediation, witness interviews, judgment about discipline, and maintaining trust with unions and management—still require human presence and accountability. Demand is relatively inelastic because it is tied to the number of unionized workplaces, contracts, disputes, and formal grievance processes rather than the price of producing more labor-relations documents. Because disruption is high while demand expansion is structurally limited, productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount needs for routine drafting, research, and case-management work even though senior human specialists remain necessary.

title: Landscape architects
rationale: Landscape architecture has a substantial digital and cognitive component: site plans, CADD models, GIS analysis, cost estimates, environmental analysis, visualizations, and client presentations are all areas where AI-assisted design and generative planning tools can materially change workflows. However, the occupation still requires licensed professional judgment, site-specific understanding, client negotiation, regulatory coordination, and occasional jobsite inspection, which limit full automation. Demand could expand somewhat as cheaper design services make professional landscape planning accessible to more homeowners, small businesses, and climate-resilience projects, but overall demand is constrained by construction budgets, land availability, permitting, and the high physical cost of implementation. Because disruption is high but elasticity is only moderate, the occupation is best characterized as restructuring rather than outright replacement or broad augmentation.

title: Lawyers
rationale: Lawyers perform a large share of tasks that are language- and knowledge-intensive, including legal research, document drafting, contract review, issue spotting, and summarizing evidence, all of which are directly in the path of current AI tools. Human lawyers will remain important for court advocacy, negotiation, client trust, ethical responsibility, and licensed legal judgment, but AI can materially reduce the labor required for many associate- and routine-practice tasks. Demand for legal help is partly suppressed by high cost, especially for individuals and small businesses, but courts, licensing rules, liability concerns, and the finite number of disputes and transactions limit how much demand can expand. Because disruption is high and elasticity is low, productivity gains are likely to reduce staffing needs in many legal workflows rather than fully translate into proportional growth in lawyer headcount.

title: Librarians and library media specialists
rationale: A large share of librarians’ core work involves information search, research assistance, cataloging, metadata, collection discovery, instruction on information resources, and evaluation of sources, all of which are directly affected by AI search, summarization, recommendation, and knowledge-management tools. However, public and school librarians also perform in-person programming, teaching, community service, supervision, and physical collection management, which prevents the disruption score from being even higher. Demand elasticity is low because most librarian employment is tied to public, school, and university budgets rather than market demand, so faster research and cataloging are unlikely to generate proportionally more funded positions. With high disruption and limited demand expansion, AI is likely to reduce staffing needs in some reference, technical-services, and research-support functions while leaving a smaller set of roles focused on instruction, curation, community programming, and complex patron support.

title: Library technicians and assistants
rationale: A substantial share of library technician and assistant work is routine information handling: catalog maintenance, circulation records, patron registration, routine reference questions, database searching, and clerical communication, all of which can be shifted toward AI search assistants, chatbots, metadata tools, and self-service systems. Some duties remain physical or interpersonal, such as shelving, helping patrons in person, and supporting community programs, which prevents a higher disruption score. Demand elasticity is low because library staffing is largely constrained by public and education budgets, physical locations, and declining library use; cheaper information assistance is unlikely to create proportionally more in-person library demand. With high disruption and low elasticity, AI-enabled automation is more likely to reduce headcount than expand the occupation.

title: Licensed practical and licensed vocational nurses
rationale: LPN/LVN work includes some cognitive and documentation tasks that AI can improve, such as charting, care-plan reminders, vital-sign monitoring, and communication with supervising clinicians. However, the core job is hands-on patient care: taking vitals, changing bandages, helping with bathing, feeding, medication support, and responding to patients in physical care settings. Demand has moderate elasticity because aging, chronic disease, and home health needs create substantial latent demand, but reimbursement, staffing rules, supervision requirements, and the inherently physical nature of care limit expansion. Because disruption remains below the high-disruption threshold, AI is likely to augment peripheral workflows rather than reshape or replace the occupation.

title: Loan officers
rationale: Loan officers perform many digital and cognitive tasks—collecting documents, verifying income and credit data, explaining loan terms, checking compliance, and applying underwriting rules—that AI and existing underwriting software can increasingly automate. Human relationship-building, sales, licensing, and judgment on complex commercial loans remain important, but routine consumer, mortgage, and underwriting workflows are directly exposed. Demand for loans would not expand proportionally if loan processing became much cheaper because borrowing is constrained by interest rates, creditworthiness, bank risk appetite, regulation, and available capital. With high disruption and limited elasticity, AI is likely to reduce headcount in routine loan origination and underwriting while leaving a smaller set of relationship-oriented and complex-credit roles.

title: Lodging managers
rationale: AI can materially affect lodging managers' administrative and analytical tasks, including revenue management, reservations, scheduling, budgeting, guest messaging, performance monitoring, and routine complaint triage. However, much of the job still depends on on-site leadership, inspecting facilities, coordinating staff in real time, handling unpredictable guest issues, and maintaining service quality in a physical environment. Demand elasticity is low because the number of lodging managers is largely tied to the number and scale of hotels, rooms, and travel demand rather than the cost of managerial tasks; cheaper management may allow some consolidation across properties rather than a large increase in consumption. Because disruption is meaningful but does not fully reshape the physical and interpersonal core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Logging workers
rationale: Logging work is overwhelmingly physical, outdoors, hazardous, and site-specific, involving chainsaws, heavy machinery, terrain judgment, equipment maintenance, and crew coordination. AI may improve peripheral or equipment-embedded functions such as route planning, machine vision for log grading, remote sensing, safety monitoring, and partial machine automation, but rugged forest environments make full substitution difficult over the next decade. Demand for logging is constrained by timber markets, land availability, environmental regulation, and sustainable harvest limits, though cheaper operations could modestly expand forest thinning and wildfire mitigation work. Because AI affects some tools and planning but does not reshape the core hands-on field work, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Logisticians
rationale: Logisticians perform substantial digital and cognitive work—forecasting demand, optimizing inventory, selecting systems, monitoring risks, analyzing costs, and coordinating suppliers—that AI can increasingly support or partially automate through predictive analytics, optimization, and automated exception management. However, the occupation also requires human judgment in real-time disruptions, supplier/customer relationships, implementation across physical operations, and tradeoffs involving risk, service levels, and organizational constraints. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper logistics analysis would let more firms optimize complex supply chains, but total demand is constrained by physical goods volumes, transportation capacity, and the need for accountable human coordination. The result is restructuring: fewer routine planning and reporting tasks, more emphasis on AI-enabled oversight, exception handling, vendor management, and strategic supply-chain design.

title: Machinists and tool and die makers
rationale: Machinists and tool and die makers use digital tools such as CAD/CAM and CNC programming, where AI can assist with toolpath generation, setup planning, inspection analysis, and troubleshooting. However, much of the core work still involves physical setup, fixturing, machine operation, material behavior, precision measurement, adjustment, and shop-floor judgment, so AI changes the workflow but does not absorb the occupation wholesale. Demand could expand somewhat if precision parts, prototyping, molds, and custom machining become cheaper, but it is constrained by downstream manufacturing demand, machine capacity, materials, and existing automation. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation fits the resilient category despite some continued automation-driven pressure on headcount.

title: Management analysts
rationale: Management analysts perform heavily cognitive, language- and data-based work: gathering documents, analyzing financial and operational data, drafting recommendations, building presentations, and writing reports, all of which AI can materially accelerate. Human judgment, client trust, interviews, onsite observation, organizational politics, and change management still matter, but much of the junior analytical and document-production workflow is in AI's direct path. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper consulting could let smaller firms, agencies, and internal teams buy or perform more operational analysis, but implementation capacity, budgets, and the need for trusted advisors limit unlimited expansion. The occupation is therefore likely to be restructured, with fewer routine analyst tasks and greater emphasis on domain expertise, client management, problem framing, and execution.

title: Manicurists and pedicurists
rationale: The core work of manicurists and pedicurists is hands-on, in-person grooming that requires fine motor control, sanitation judgment, client interaction, and adaptation to individual hands, feet, nails, and skin. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as appointment scheduling, design inspiration, marketing, inventory, and perhaps limited robotic polish application, but it does not substantially replace the full service experience. Demand would expand somewhat if services became much faster or cheaper, especially through quick manicures, mobile services, and broader use by price-sensitive customers, but grooming frequency and the desire for human service limit elasticity. Because disruption to the core occupation is low, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Marine engineers and naval architects
rationale: Marine engineering and naval architecture involve substantial digital knowledge work: CAD drawings, schematics, hydrodynamic and structural analysis, cost estimates, specifications, compliance documentation, and technical reports are all areas where AI and generative design tools can materially accelerate work. Disruption is not higher because the occupation also requires safety-critical engineering judgment, regulatory accountability, prototype testing, shipyard coordination, and some on-site or offshore presence. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper design could enable more optimization, emissions retrofits, offshore wind platforms, and customized vessel designs, but total demand is constrained by capital-intensive shipbuilding, government procurement, regulation, and shipyard capacity. Because AI changes many core design and analysis tasks but demand expansion is only partial, the occupation is best categorized as restructure.

title: Market research analysts
rationale: Market research analysts perform highly digital and cognitive work: designing surveys, gathering online and competitive data, analyzing datasets, forecasting trends, and producing reports and presentations. Generative AI and analytics tools can already automate or accelerate survey drafting, sentiment analysis, segmentation, dashboarding, visualization, and first-draft insight generation, though human judgment remains important for research design, client context, and strategic interpretation. Demand should expand because cheaper research enables more firms, products, campaigns, and customer segments to be analyzed, but it is limited by marketing budgets, managerial decision capacity, and the fact that not every business question needs extensive research. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is best classified as restructure: fewer workers will be needed for routine analysis and reporting, while demand rises for analysts who can frame problems, validate AI outputs, and translate findings into business strategy.

title: Marriage and family therapists
rationale: Marriage and family therapy is largely language-based cognitive work: assessment, guided conversation, treatment planning, documentation, and follow-up are all areas where AI can materially assist or partially automate. However, the occupation still depends heavily on trust, rapport, clinical judgment, crisis recognition, ethics, and licensure, so AI is more likely to reshape delivery than fully replace therapists. Demand elasticity is high because mental health and relationship counseling have substantial unmet demand due to cost, provider shortages, scheduling barriers, and stigma, and cheaper AI-enabled services would likely bring many more people into care. Because disruption is high but latent demand is also high, AI is likely to augment therapists through blended care, documentation automation, triage, and between-session support rather than cause broad headcount contraction.

title: Masonry workers
rationale: Masonry is overwhelmingly physical, site-specific work involving lifting, cutting, placing, aligning, finishing, and repairing heavy materials in variable outdoor and construction-site conditions. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as blueprint interpretation, estimating materials, scheduling, layout guidance, and possibly some robotic or prefabrication workflows, but it does not substantially take over the core hands-on craft in the next decade. Demand would expand somewhat if masonry became much cheaper, especially for repairs, decorative work, and substitution back toward brick or stone, but construction is constrained by land, permitting, project financing, and broader building demand. Because disruption to the core occupation is low-to-moderate, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Massage therapists
rationale: Massage therapy is overwhelmingly hands-on, physical, and presence-based, with core tasks requiring tactile assessment, manual dexterity, client comfort, and real-time adjustment to the body. AI may help with scheduling, documentation, marketing, intake forms, or exercise/stretching suggestions, and robotic massage devices may improve, but these do not substitute for most licensed therapeutic massage work over the next decade. Demand is moderately elastic because lower prices or easier access could increase frequency of wellness, pain-management, and relaxation services, but consumption is limited by session time, trust, human-touch preferences, and physical delivery constraints. Because disruption to the core work is low, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Material moving machine operators
rationale: The work is primarily physical and site-based, involving safe operation of forklifts, cranes, conveyors, hoists, and dredging equipment around people, loads, and changing real-world conditions. However, AI-enabled warehouse automation, autonomous mobile robots, automated forklifts, sensors, scanners, and routing systems can increasingly take over or reshape some core material-moving tasks, especially in structured warehouses. Demand is relatively inelastic because material moving is derived from goods production, warehousing, construction, and shipping volumes; cheaper operation may support e-commerce and logistics growth but will not cause society to move 10 times more physical material. Because disruption is moderate rather than high across the occupation as a whole, the net effect is resilient, though some warehouse and conveyor roles may face localized automation pressure.

title: Material recording clerks
rationale: Material recording clerks perform many routine, structured tasks—inventory records, shipment verification, scheduling updates, reports, invoices, and exception tracking—that are directly automatable with AI-enabled warehouse management systems, RFID, computer vision, and automated storage tools. Some work still requires physical presence, such as inspecting damage, labeling packages, sampling materials, or moving goods, which keeps disruption below the highest levels. Demand elasticity is low because the need for inventory and shipment recordkeeping is tied mainly to the volume of physical goods, not to the price of clerical labor; cheaper recordkeeping will not cause firms to need many more clerks. Because disruption is high and demand expansion is limited, productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount, making the net effect replace.

title: Materials engineers
rationale: Materials engineering has a large cognitive and computational component: literature review, simulation, property prediction, experimental design, failure analysis, report writing, and materials selection are all areas where AI and machine learning can materially change workflows. However, the occupation still depends on physical testing, lab and factory validation, qualification, safety judgment, and collaboration with manufacturing and product teams, so AI is unlikely to fully automate the role. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper materials discovery would unlock more work in batteries, semiconductors, aerospace, sustainability, and advanced manufacturing, but adoption is constrained by physical experimentation, capital equipment, certification cycles, and downstream production timelines. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is best classified as restructure.

title: Mathematicians and statisticians
rationale: Mathematicians and statisticians perform highly digital, cognitive work involving modeling, coding, data analysis, visualization, and written interpretation, all areas where AI tools are already materially useful. However, the occupation still requires expert judgment in study design, causal reasoning, assumptions, uncertainty, data validity, and communicating limitations in high-stakes contexts such as healthcare, government, and R&D. Demand should expand as cheaper analysis lets more organizations run experiments, analyze data, and build statistical models, but growth is moderated by data quality, regulation, trust requirements, and the ability of non-specialists to use AI tools directly. The result is substantial restructuring: routine analysis and reporting are automated, while demand shifts toward statisticians who can frame problems, validate models, govern methods, and translate results into decisions.

title: Mechanical engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: AI will materially affect the digital and analytical parts of this occupation, including CAD drafting, design checking, documentation, calculations, simulation support, and test-data analysis. However, a large share of the job still involves hands-on setup, measurement, prototyping, troubleshooting, inspection, and coordination in labs or manufacturing environments, which limits full automation over the next decade. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper design and testing support could enable more prototyping and product iteration, but demand is constrained by physical production cycles, capital equipment, safety requirements, and manufacturing volumes. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the entire core of the job, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Mechanical engineers
rationale: Mechanical engineers perform substantial digital and cognitive work—CAD modeling, simulation, analysis, design iteration, documentation, and failure diagnosis—that AI copilots, generative design tools, and automated simulation workflows can materially accelerate. However, the occupation is not fully automatable because prototypes, testing, manufacturing constraints, safety, regulation, and cross-functional engineering judgment remain tied to physical systems and real-world accountability. Demand should expand meaningfully as cheaper engineering enables more product iteration, automation, robotics, energy systems, and customized machinery, but growth is limited by capital costs, manufacturing lead times, certification, and physical deployment constraints. Because disruption is high but elasticity is only moderate, the occupation is best categorized as restructure: fewer engineers may be needed for routine design and analysis, while demand rises for those who can use AI tools, validate outputs, integrate systems, and manage complex physical engineering tradeoffs.

title: Medical and health services managers
rationale: Medical and health services managers do substantial digital and cognitive work—budgeting, scheduling, compliance tracking, reporting, billing oversight, and EHR-related analysis—that AI can materially streamline. However, the core role also depends on human leadership, staff supervision, regulatory accountability, conflict resolution, patient and clinician interaction, and on-site crisis management in complex healthcare settings. Demand elasticity is moderate because aging populations, healthcare complexity, and smaller practices' need for better administration create some room for expanded management services, but demand is constrained by the number of facilities, clinical staff, regulations, and patients. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape or absorb the whole occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Medical assistants
rationale: Medical assistants combine automatable administrative work—scheduling, phone intake, insurance forms, coding support, and EHR data entry—with hands-on clinical tasks such as taking vitals, preparing specimens, giving injections where permitted, and assisting patients and physicians in person. AI and automation will materially reduce documentation and front-office workload, but much of the occupation still depends on physical presence, patient interaction, and regulated clinical support. Demand has moderate elasticity because aging populations and primary-care access constraints create real need for more visits, but expansion is limited by physician capacity, reimbursement, regulation, and the need for in-person care. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the entire core of the job, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Medical dosimetrists
rationale: Medical dosimetry is highly computer-based and centered on image review, dose calculation, treatment-plan optimization, documentation, and quality checks, all areas where AI-assisted contouring, auto-planning, and verification tools are already advancing. Human expertise will remain important because the work is safety-critical, regulated, and integrated with physicians, physicists, and radiation therapists, but the core technical planning workflow is directly in AI’s path. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of radiation treatment plans is driven mainly by cancer incidence, physician prescriptions, equipment capacity, and clinical protocols rather than the cost or speed of dosimetry alone. Since AI can substantially reduce planning labor while cheaper planning is unlikely to generate enough additional treatment volume, the occupation fits the replace category.

title: Medical equipment repairers
rationale: AI will materially help with diagnostic support, technical manuals, remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, recordkeeping, software updates, and troubleshooting workflows. However, the core job still requires on-site physical work: installing equipment, testing and calibrating devices, replacing parts, using tools, moving equipment, and ensuring safety in clinical environments. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper maintenance could enable more preventive service and support a growing installed base of medical devices, but total demand is still constrained by healthcare facilities, regulation, and the physical stock of equipment. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Medical records specialists
rationale: Medical records specialists perform predominantly digital, rules-based, language-heavy work: extracting information from clinical notes, checking completeness, assigning billing and diagnosis codes, and entering data into EHR systems. AI systems are already well suited to clinical documentation review, automated coding suggestions, error detection, and record retrieval, with humans increasingly shifting toward exception handling, audits, and compliance oversight. Demand is relatively inelastic because the volume of medical records is tied mainly to healthcare encounters, regulation, and reimbursement workflows rather than the price of coding labor, although aging and chronic disease will add some baseline growth. Because disruption is very high and cheaper coding is unlikely to create enough new work to offset automation, the occupation fits the replace category.

title: Medical scientists
rationale: Medical scientists do substantial cognitive and digital work—literature review, hypothesis generation, study design, statistical analysis, grant writing, publication, drug discovery, and interpretation of clinical or molecular data—that AI can already materially accelerate. Disruption is not higher because much of the occupation remains tied to wet-lab experimentation, clinical trials, biological uncertainty, safety procedures, regulatory requirements, and expert scientific judgment. Demand elasticity is high because biomedical research has enormous unmet demand in cancer, Alzheimer’s, chronic disease, antimicrobial resistance, rare diseases, and personalized medicine, so cheaper research would likely expand the number of questions, targets, and therapies pursued. The net effect is augment: AI will substantially change workflows and required skills, but expanded research output and persistent health needs should absorb much of the productivity gain rather than simply reduce headcount.

title: Medical transcriptionists
rationale: Medical transcription is almost entirely digital, language-based work: listening to dictation, converting it into text, editing drafts, and entering documentation into EHR systems. Speech recognition, natural language processing, and ambient clinical documentation tools already perform much of the core task, with humans increasingly limited to exception handling, quality review, and compliance-sensitive edits. Demand is relatively inelastic because the volume of medical transcription is tied to patient encounters and required documentation, and cheaper transcription does not cause physicians or patients to consume vastly more reports. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity means productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount, so the net effect is replace.

title: Meeting, convention, and event planners
rationale: AI can substantially assist the digital and cognitive parts of event planning, including drafting schedules, budgets, proposals, vendor comparisons, attendee communications, registration workflows, surveys, and contingency plans. However, the core job still depends heavily on client trust, negotiation, relationship management, venue inspection, vendor coordination, and real-time problem-solving at unpredictable in-person events. Demand has moderate elasticity: cheaper planning tools could let more small businesses, nonprofits, couples, and community groups use professional planning support, but the number and scale of events remain constrained by budgets, calendars, venues, and social need. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to displace the human-centered and on-site core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Metal and plastic machine workers
rationale: AI and adjacent automation will materially affect machine monitoring, CNC programming, toolpath generation, visual inspection, predictive maintenance, and the ability of one operator to oversee multiple machines. However, much of the occupation still requires physical setup, loading and unloading materials, changing tools, troubleshooting equipment, measuring parts, and maintaining safety around real machines, which keeps disruption below the high-disruption threshold. Demand for machined metal and plastic parts would expand somewhat if production became cheaper, especially through reshoring and more customization, but it is constrained by downstream product demand, materials costs, capital equipment, and global competition. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best categorized as resilient, even though employment may continue to decline from broader factory automation.

title: Microbiologists
rationale: Microbiologists perform substantial cognitive and digital work—literature review, experimental design, bioinformatics, image analysis, technical writing, and grant/report preparation—that AI can materially accelerate. However, the core occupation still depends heavily on wet-lab work, culturing organisms, specimen handling, safety protocols, equipment use, and real-world experimental judgment, limiting full automation over the next decade. Demand could expand meaningfully in drug discovery, infectious disease surveillance, environmental monitoring, industrial biotech, and synthetic biology if research becomes cheaper, but it remains constrained by lab capacity, regulation, funding, and long development timelines. Because disruption is significant but not high enough to fully reshape the hands-on core of the job, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Middle school teachers
rationale: AI can substantially assist middle school teachers with lesson planning, differentiated materials, grading, feedback, parent communication, and individualized practice, so a meaningful share of the cognitive and administrative workload is exposed. However, the core job also involves in-person classroom management, motivation, supervision, adolescent development, relationship-building, and legal/custodial responsibilities that are difficult to automate. Demand elasticity is limited because the number of middle school students is largely fixed by demographics and public school staffing is constrained by budgets, class-size rules, and regulation, though cheaper AI-enabled instruction could modestly expand tutoring and personalization. Because disruption is meaningful but the core occupation still requires human presence and authority, the occupation is best classified as resilient rather than replaced.

title: Military careers
rationale: AI will materially change many military tasks, especially intelligence analysis, surveillance, targeting support, logistics, cyber operations, simulation-based training, maintenance, and administrative work. However, the occupation as a whole still requires physical readiness, deployment, command responsibility, teamwork, security presence, and human accountability in unpredictable and dangerous environments. Demand for military personnel is relatively inelastic because force size is driven by national security strategy, budgets, law, and geopolitical threats rather than the unit cost of producing military output. Because disruption is substantial but still low-to-moderate for the broad occupation, the net effect is resilient rather than replacement.

title: Mining and geological engineers
rationale: AI can substantially assist the digital and analytical parts of mining and geological engineering, including geological modeling, mine-plan optimization, production monitoring, environmental analysis, safety documentation, and technical report drafting. However, the occupation still depends heavily on site-specific engineering judgment, field conditions, regulatory accountability, worker safety, construction oversight, and coordination with physical mining operations, so AI is unlikely to absorb the core role end-to-end. Demand elasticity is limited because the number of mines, mineral deposits, permits, capital projects, and commodity-driven extraction decisions will not expand dramatically just because engineering analysis is cheaper. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient rather than replaced or restructured.

title: Models
rationale: A large share of modeling work for catalogs, online ads, product promotion, and portfolio-based casting is visual content production, which is directly affected by generative AI, virtual models, image editing, and reuse of existing likenesses. Human presence remains important for runway shows, live events, fit modeling, trade shows, and some brand campaigns, so disruption is high but not total. Demand for modeled imagery may expand as ads become cheaper to produce, but much of that expansion can be served by synthetic or reused images rather than additional human models. Because disruption is high and elasticity for human headcount is low, the occupation fits the replace category.

title: Music directors and composers
rationale: AI music-generation and audio-production tools already affect composing, arranging, lyric drafting, demo creation, orchestration, and promotional materials, putting a large share of the composer side directly in AI’s path. Music directors and conductors are less automatable because rehearsals, live performance leadership, interpersonal coaching, auditions, and community presence still require human judgment and embodied authority. Demand could expand for inexpensive custom music in video, games, advertising, social media, churches, and small productions, but it is limited by attention scarcity, nonprofit and school funding constraints, and continued preference for human-led live performance. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is likely to restructure rather than broadly disappear or grow unchanged.

title: Musicians and singers
rationale: AI music generation, voice synthesis, mixing tools, and promotional automation will materially affect recording, demo production, background vocals, session work, and self-marketing. However, much of the occupation is live, embodied performance where audience demand is tied to authenticity, stage presence, reputation, and social experience rather than just the sound output. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper production will create more music and content, but listener attention, venue capacity, church participation, and arts budgets limit how much additional demand translates into paid human musician jobs. Because disruption is significant but the core live-performance role remains only moderately reshaped, the occupation fits the resilient category.

title: Natural sciences managers
rationale: Natural sciences managers perform substantial cognitive and language-based work—setting research strategy, reviewing scientific work, drafting reports, budgeting, coordinating teams, and communicating with executives or clients—all areas where AI tools can materially improve speed and scope. However, the role also depends on human leadership, accountability, personnel management, lab safety, regulatory judgment, and coordination in physical research or production environments, so AI is unlikely to replace the full managerial function. Demand for scientific R&D and product development could expand as AI lowers the cost of experimentation and analysis, but it is constrained by funding, regulation, physical lab capacity, and organizations’ ability to widen managerial spans of control. The occupation is therefore likely to be substantially restructured, with fewer purely administrative managers and greater value placed on those who can use AI to oversee larger, more complex scientific programs.

title: Network and computer systems administrators
rationale: Network and computer systems administration is heavily digital and rule-based: monitoring alerts, diagnosing incidents, configuring systems, scripting automation, managing permissions, patching, and documenting changes are all areas where AI and AIOps tools can materially improve productivity. Some work still requires human judgment, accountability, security oversight, vendor coordination, and occasional physical presence for hardware or network infrastructure, but the core workflow is increasingly automated, cloud-managed, and software-defined. Demand elasticity is limited because most organizations need a reliable baseline of administration rather than vastly more administration when it becomes cheaper; productivity gains are likely absorbed through fewer admins per server, network, or user, plus outsourcing to managed and cloud services. Given high disruption and relatively low demand expansion, the occupation fits the replace category, especially for routine systems and network administration roles.

title: News analysts, reporters, and journalists
rationale: Journalism has substantial digital, cognitive, and language-based work: researching background material, drafting articles and scripts, summarizing updates, editing for style, creating headlines, and repurposing content across platforms are all directly affected by current AI tools. Human reporters remain important for source development, interviews, field presence, judgment, verification, and accountability, but many newsroom production tasks can be accelerated or partially automated. Demand elasticity is limited because news consumption is constrained by audience attention, trust, and weak advertising/subscription economics, though cheaper AI-enabled production may expand some niche and hyperlocal coverage. Given high disruption and relatively low elasticity, AI is likely to reduce headcount in routine reporting and content-production roles while leaving a smaller set of journalists focused on original reporting, verification, and distinctive analysis.

title: Nuclear engineers
rationale: Nuclear engineering includes substantial digital and cognitive work—simulation, calculations, design documentation, regulatory analysis, and technical writing—so AI can materially improve productivity in modeling, code generation, optimization, and compliance drafting. However, the core work is safety-critical, highly regulated, tied to physical facilities and experiments, and requires accountable human engineering judgment, which limits full automation over the next decade. Demand elasticity is low because the number of nuclear projects is constrained more by regulation, capital costs, public policy, construction timelines, and federal or utility budgets than by the cost of engineering labor alone. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient rather than replace or restructure.

title: Nuclear medicine technologists
rationale: Nuclear medicine technologists perform some digital and cognitive tasks—dose calculations, equipment operation, imaging workflows, documentation, and quality control—that AI can assist through automation, image acquisition support, scheduling, and error checking. However, the core job remains hands-on and regulated: preparing and administering radioactive drugs, positioning and monitoring patients, following radiation-safety protocols, and responding to clinical situations in person. Demand would expand only modestly if workflows became cheaper or faster because use is constrained by medical necessity, radiation exposure, physician orders, reimbursement, equipment capacity, and licensing rules, though aging-related cancer care and theranostics create some growth. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment peripheral and technical tasks than replace the occupation, making the net effect resilient.

title: Nuclear technicians
rationale: AI can materially improve monitoring, anomaly detection, radiation-data analysis, predictive maintenance, documentation, and procedure guidance, but much of the occupation still requires onsite presence, calibrated instruments, sampling, equipment maintenance, safety compliance, and incident response in regulated facilities. The core work is therefore only moderately disrupted rather than fully automatable. Demand is quite inelastic because staffing is tied to the number of nuclear plants, labs, waste sites, and regulatory safety requirements, not to consumer demand for more technician output. Because disruption is below the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite weak demand elasticity.

title: Nurse anesthetists, nurse midwives, and nurse practitioners
rationale: AI will materially assist APRNs with documentation, clinical decision support, diagnostic interpretation, patient messaging, risk stratification, and care-plan generation, but the core work still involves in-person assessment, procedures, medication management, anesthesia monitoring, childbirth care, and regulated clinical judgment. The occupation requires physical presence, trust-building, liability-bearing decisions, and hands-on response to unpredictable patient conditions, limiting full automation over the next decade. Demand elasticity is high because primary care, chronic disease management, behavioral health, maternal care, and anesthesia services face substantial access constraints, and cheaper AI-enabled care could expand visits, monitoring, and preventive services. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment APRNs at the margins and improve throughput than to fundamentally replace or restructure the occupation.

title: Nursing assistants and orderlies
rationale: Core tasks for nursing assistants and orderlies are highly physical, hands-on, and presence-based: bathing, feeding, toileting, repositioning, transporting, cleaning, and observing patients in real environments. AI can help with documentation, scheduling, monitoring, fall detection, translation, and some robotic transport or lifting assistance, but it is not close to replacing the interpersonal and unpredictable bedside care at scale. Demand elasticity is fairly high because elder care and long-term care are strongly constrained by labor cost, staffing shortages, and reimbursement limits, so cheaper care could increase staffing ratios, home-based services, and access. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite meaningful latent demand, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Occupational health and safety specialists and technicians
rationale: AI can materially assist the digital and cognitive parts of this job, including regulatory research, incident trend analysis, risk scoring, report drafting, training materials, and sensor or computer-vision monitoring. However, much of the core work still requires on-site inspection, physical testing, worker interaction, judgment in hazardous or changing environments, and accountability for regulatory compliance. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper safety analysis could let more small employers, construction sites, and manufacturers conduct more frequent audits, but demand is constrained by regulation, workplace count, and the need for physical presence. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with AI augmenting documentation and analytics more than replacing the role.

title: Occupational therapists
rationale: Occupational therapy has meaningful cognitive and documentation components where AI can help, such as drafting notes, suggesting treatment plans, analyzing progress data, and supporting home-accessibility recommendations. However, the core work depends heavily on in-person assessment, hands-on demonstration, physical assistance, patient motivation, family education, and adaptation to real-world home, school, or clinical environments. Demand would likely expand moderately if services became cheaper because aging, disability, autism, stroke recovery, and home-care needs are substantial, but licensing, reimbursement, and the need for human clinical presence limit scalability. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and AI mostly augments peripheral and planning tasks rather than replacing the therapeutic relationship and hands-on care, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Occupational therapy assistants and aides
rationale: AI can help with documentation, scheduling, insurance forms, progress tracking, home-exercise reminders, and decision support for therapy plans, but the core work involves hands-on guidance, observing movement, motivating patients, setting up equipment, and often physically assisting people in clinical or home settings. Robotics and remote monitoring may improve productivity, but they are not close to replacing the interpersonal, physical, and safety-sensitive parts of occupational therapy assistance. Demand is moderately elastic because aging populations, rehabilitation needs, and cost constraints create latent demand, but insurance reimbursement, licensing rules, and the need for in-person care limit how much consumption can expand. Because disruption is low-to-moderate rather than high, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Oil and gas workers
rationale: Oil and gas workers perform mostly physical, onsite tasks: assembling, operating, inspecting, repairing, loading, cleaning, and moving heavy equipment in hazardous and variable environments. AI, sensors, automated drilling, robotics, and remote monitoring can change some drilling, monitoring, maintenance, and coordination tasks, but much of the core work still requires human presence, mechanical judgment, and hands-on intervention. Demand elasticity is low because oil and gas output is constrained by energy demand, commodity prices, reserves, regulation, and capital investment; cheaper labor or faster operations would not cause society to consume vastly more oil and gas. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient, even though productivity improvements may limit job growth.

title: Operations research analysts
rationale: Operations research analysts do predominantly digital, quantitative, and language-based work: collecting data, building models, running forecasts/optimizations, coding analytical tools, and writing recommendations. AI can already accelerate data cleaning, model development, simulation, coding, visualization, and report drafting, although humans remain important for problem framing, stakeholder interviews, validating assumptions, and persuading decision-makers. Demand elasticity is high because many organizations currently underuse advanced optimization due to cost, expertise, and implementation barriers; cheaper AI-assisted analysis would expand use across logistics, pricing, staffing, healthcare, government, and small-to-mid-sized firms. Because disruption is high but cheaper analysis is likely to unlock substantial additional demand, the occupation is best categorized as augment rather than replace.

title: Opticians
rationale: Opticians have some digital and cognitive tasks that AI can improve, such as interpreting prescriptions, recommending frames or lens options, creating work orders, managing inventory, and supporting online or virtual try-on sales. However, much of the core job remains hands-on and customer-facing, including taking precise measurements, fitting and adjusting frames, repairing eyewear, and teaching contact lens use. Demand is only modestly elastic because eyewear needs are driven mainly by prescriptions, aging, and vision problems, though lower costs and better online tools may increase purchases of extra pairs or customized options. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Optometrists
rationale: Optometry has a substantial diagnostic and cognitive component—interpreting vision tests, retinal images, patient history, and treatment options—that AI can increasingly assist through automated refraction, image analysis, triage, and documentation. However, the core job still requires licensed clinical judgment, patient interaction, hands-on examination, fitting and prescribing decisions, and in some cases medication or procedures, so AI is more likely to reshape workflows than replace the clinician. Demand could expand moderately if exams and screening become cheaper, especially for aging patients, diabetic eye monitoring, myopia management, and underserved populations, but most people do not need unlimited eye exams and reimbursement/regulation constrain volume. Because disruption is meaningful but still below the high-disruption threshold, the occupation fits the resilient category.

title: Orthotists and prosthetists
rationale: AI will affect important parts of orthotics and prosthetics, especially digital scanning, CAD/CAM design, gait analysis, materials selection, documentation, and potentially automated fabrication through 3D printing. However, the core work still depends heavily on in-person patient assessment, hands-on fitting, iterative adjustment, clinical judgment, dexterity, and communication with patients who have complex physical needs. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper and faster customization could expand access, enable more frequent replacement or upgrading of devices, and increase use of custom orthoses, but demand is still constrained by medical need, insurance reimbursement, and clinical workflows. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the occupation’s core hands-on clinical role, the net effect is resilient.

title: Painters, construction and maintenance
rationale: Painting is overwhelmingly physical, site-specific work involving surface preparation, masking, climbing, spraying or brushing, and quality control in varied real-world environments. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as estimating paint quantities, scheduling, customer visualization, bidding, and possibly limited robotic spraying in controlled settings, but it does not materially replace the core hands-on work over the next decade. If painting became much cheaper, some homeowners and property owners would repaint more often or outsource work they currently do themselves, but demand is still constrained by the stock of buildings, construction cycles, materials, and the practical need for onsite work. Because disruption is low despite moderate demand elasticity, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Painting and coating workers
rationale: The work is heavily physical and machine-based: preparing surfaces, positioning items, operating spray or coating equipment, inspecting finish quality, and cleaning tools and booths. AI-enabled machine vision, robotic spray systems, and process optimization can improve quality control and automate some setup or monitoring, especially in large manufacturing plants, but much of the job still involves hands-on materials handling, equipment maintenance, touch-up work, and shop-floor presence. Demand is relatively inelastic because coatings are a derived need tied to the number of cars, furniture, metal products, and other goods being produced or repaired; making coating much cheaper would not cause consumers to buy vastly more coated products. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate rather than primarily digital or cognitive, the net effect is resilient despite ongoing industrial automation pressure.

title: Paralegals and legal assistants
rationale: Paralegal work is heavily composed of digital, language-based tasks such as legal research, document review, drafting correspondence and filings, organizing case materials, and summarizing transcripts, all of which are directly exposed to current AI tools. Some tasks involving client coordination, affidavits, trial logistics, and attorney judgment still require human oversight, but the core productivity bottleneck is highly automatable. Demand for legal help is partly suppressed by cost, but courts, attorney supervision requirements, unauthorized-practice rules, and case volumes limit how much cheaper paralegal output can expand total work. Because disruption is very high and elasticity is low, AI is likely to reduce headcount needs substantially even as remaining paralegals become more productive.

title: Personal financial advisors
rationale: Personal financial advising is heavily cognitive and language-based: gathering client facts, explaining options, modeling retirement scenarios, researching investments, monitoring portfolios, and drafting plans are all tasks AI can materially accelerate. However, the occupation also depends on trust, sales, regulatory accountability, and emotionally sensitive judgment around life events, which limits full automation. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper advice could open the market to younger, lower-wealth, and mass-affluent clients who currently do not pay for human planning, but high-net-worth and complex cases remain relationship-driven and regulated. Because disruption is high while demand expansion is meaningful but not enough to fully absorb productivity gains, the occupation is best classified as restructure.

title: Pest control workers
rationale: Pest control work is heavily physical and location-specific: workers inspect buildings, crawl through tight spaces, set traps, apply pesticides, seal entry points, and interact with customers on-site. AI can improve peripheral and knowledge tasks such as scheduling, route optimization, recordkeeping, pest identification from photos, treatment recommendations, and remote monitoring via smart traps, but it does not replace the core hands-on work. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper service could expand preventive treatments and monitoring subscriptions, especially for homeowners and commercial properties, but total demand is still constrained by actual infestation rates, safety regulation, and the need for physical service visits. Because disruption is low-to-moderate, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Petroleum engineers
rationale: Petroleum engineering is heavily analytical and model-based: reservoir simulation, drilling optimization, production forecasting, equipment monitoring, and technical reporting are all areas where AI and advanced analytics can materially improve productivity. The disruption is not higher because engineers still need field judgment, safety accountability, coordination with crews, and decisions tied to physical assets and uncertain subsurface conditions. Demand elasticity is low because demand for petroleum engineering is ultimately constrained by oil and gas prices, reserves, capital budgets, regulation, and the energy transition; cheaper engineering does not create 10x more drilling or production activity. Given high disruption and limited expansion in total demand, AI is likely to reduce headcount needs while leaving a smaller set of engineers focused on oversight, complex troubleshooting, and integration with field operations.

title: Pharmacists
rationale: Pharmacists perform many cognitive and information-intensive tasks—checking interactions, verifying doses, counseling patients, maintaining records, resolving insurance issues, and advising clinicians—that AI and clinical decision-support systems can substantially augment or partially automate. However, the occupation also has regulated, high-liability, patient-facing, and hands-on components such as vaccinations, controlled dispensing, supervision, and clinical accountability, which limit full replacement. Demand could expand moderately through cheaper medication therapy management, chronic disease support, adherence monitoring, and access in clinics or underserved areas, but prescription volume and pharmacist scope are constrained by regulation, insurer reimbursement, and healthcare utilization. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is best classified as restructure.

title: Pharmacy technicians
rationale: Pharmacy technicians have a meaningful digital and routine component—entering patient data, processing insurance claims, handling refill requests, inventory tracking, and answering basic customer questions—that AI and pharmacy automation can streamline. However, much of the core work still requires regulated, in-person handling of medications, packaging, labeling, customer interaction, hospital rounds, and supervision by pharmacists, so AI is more likely to change workflows than fully absorb the job. Demand is relatively inelastic because prescription volume is driven mainly by demographics, chronic disease, and medical need rather than the cost of technician labor, though some additional medication-management and pharmacy-service demand may be unlocked. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation fits the resilient category despite some automation pressure.

title: Phlebotomists
rationale: Phlebotomy is primarily hands-on, physical clinical work involving venipuncture, patient reassurance, specimen handling, sanitation, and real-world presence. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as scheduling, identity verification, documentation, labeling checks, and possibly vein visualization or robotic assistance, but widespread autonomous blood draws face safety, liability, patient-comfort, and workflow barriers. Demand would expand only modestly if draws became cheaper or faster because blood testing is driven by medical need, clinician orders, insurance coverage, and lab capacity rather than pure consumer demand. Because disruption to the core task remains low-to-moderate, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.

title: Photographers
rationale: AI will substantially affect photographers’ digital workflow, especially culling, retouching, color correction, background replacement, portfolio management, marketing, and in some commercial uses the creation of synthetic images that substitute for shoots. However, much of the occupation still depends on being physically present at weddings, portraits, news events, schools, real estate sites, or commercial locations, plus directing subjects, managing lighting, and handling clients in real time. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper image production would increase visual content for ecommerce, advertising, social media, and small businesses, but demand for event and portrait photography is constrained by the number of real occasions and clients’ desire for authentic images. Because disruption is meaningful but not enough to fully reshape the physical, interpersonal core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Physical therapist assistants and aides
rationale: AI can affect documentation, scheduling, insurance forms, patient education, exercise reminders, and remote monitoring, but the core work involves hands-on patient assistance, manual therapy, gait and balance training, equipment setup, cleaning, and physically helping patients move. Over the next decade, AI-enabled rehab tools and computer vision may improve supervision and home exercise adherence, but they are unlikely to replace the in-person, licensed, compassionate, physically interactive role of physical therapist assistants and aides. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower-cost therapy could expand access for aging patients, chronic disease management, post-injury rehabilitation, and home-based care, though insurance reimbursement, clinical supervision rules, and the finite need for therapy sessions limit expansion. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate and the core occupation is anchored in physical patient care, the net effect is resilient.

title: Physical therapists
rationale: Physical therapy includes substantial cognitive work—assessment, care-plan design, documentation, patient education, and progress monitoring—that AI can assist through automated notes, exercise-plan generation, computer-vision movement analysis, and remote coaching. However, the core of the occupation remains hands-on, licensed, relational, and physically present, especially for manual therapy, safe mobility training, and adapting treatment to pain, frailty, or complex conditions. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper, AI-supported therapy could expand access for chronic pain, aging-related mobility issues, post-surgical rehab, and preventive care, but use is still constrained by insurance coverage, referrals, patient time, and the need for in-person treatment. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment peripheral and monitoring tasks than replace the central clinical role, making the occupation resilient.

title: Physician assistants
rationale: AI will substantially affect the cognitive and administrative parts of physician assistant work, including documentation, clinical decision support, test interpretation, differential diagnosis, patient education, and treatment planning. However, the core role still requires licensed clinical judgment, physical examination, procedures, prescribing responsibility, patient trust, and in-person care in unpredictable settings such as clinics, hospitals, emergency departments, and surgery. Demand elasticity is high because healthcare access is constrained by cost, provider shortages, aging demographics, chronic disease, and underserved communities, so productivity gains would likely be absorbed into more visits, monitoring, and preventive care. Because disruption is meaningful but not enough to displace the hands-on licensed clinical core, the occupation fits the resilient category.

title: Physicians and surgeons
rationale: AI will substantially affect physicians' cognitive and administrative work, including documentation, triage, diagnostic support, test interpretation, care-plan drafting, and patient communication. However, the occupation still depends heavily on licensed clinical judgment, physical examination, procedures, surgery, bedside interaction, liability-bearing decisions, and coordination in unpredictable real-world settings, so AI is more likely to reshape workflows than absorb the full role. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper physician input would unlock some latent demand in primary care, chronic disease management, mental health, and underserved areas, but utilization is constrained by insurance, regulation, facilities, patient capacity, and the fact that many services are medically rather than consumer-demand driven. Because disruption is significant but not above the high-disruption threshold for the broad occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Physicists and astronomers
rationale: Physicists and astronomers do a large amount of digital and cognitive work—mathematical modeling, coding, simulation, literature review, data analysis, proposal writing, and scientific publishing—where AI tools can materially accelerate workflows. However, the occupation also depends on frontier scientific judgment, experimental design, specialized instruments, laboratory or observatory access, and peer validation, which limits full automation. Demand could expand in applied areas such as materials, quantum technologies, medical physics, fusion, and space science, but academic and federal research funding, facility bottlenecks, and grant structures constrain how much cheaper analysis translates into more headcount. The result is substantial restructuring of skills and workflows rather than straightforward replacement or broad employment expansion.

title: Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters
rationale: The core work of plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters is hands-on installation, repair, inspection, troubleshooting, lifting, fitting, welding, and working in variable physical environments such as homes, factories, crawlspaces, and construction sites. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as estimating, scheduling, code lookup, blueprint/BIM review, diagnostics, customer communication, and inventory planning, but it is not close to replacing the manual dexterity and on-site judgment required for most jobs. Demand would expand somewhat if services became cheaper and faster, especially for deferred maintenance, renovations, and proactive inspections, but it is constrained by the stock of buildings, construction activity, codes, and the physical need for on-site labor. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and AI mainly augments administrative and planning tasks rather than reshaping the core trade, the occupation is resilient.

title: Podiatrists
rationale: Podiatrists do use cognitive medical judgment, imaging review, documentation, prescribing, and patient education, all of which AI can assist through decision support, charting, triage, and diagnostic aids. However, the core occupation remains heavily grounded in in-person physical exams, hands-on treatment, wound care, procedures, surgery, and licensed clinical responsibility, so AI is unlikely to absorb the central work over the next decade. Demand could expand moderately if AI-enabled tools make screening, orthotics, documentation, and follow-up cheaper, especially for diabetes, obesity, aging-related mobility problems, and underserved patients, but utilization is still limited by insurance, referrals, patient visits, and substitution by other clinicians. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Police and detectives
rationale: AI can materially assist with report writing, transcription, database searches, surveillance review, evidence triage, dispatch support, and investigative pattern analysis. However, the core of policing still requires unpredictable real-world presence, legal authority, physical intervention, de-escalation, judgment under uncertainty, arrests, testimony, and public accountability. Demand for police services is relatively inelastic because staffing is driven by public safety needs, law, politics, and government budgets rather than by the marginal cost of producing reports or investigations. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is likely to change tools and workflows more than replace the central human role.

title: Political scientists
rationale: Political scientists perform predominantly digital, cognitive, and language-heavy work: collecting and analyzing survey and policy data, monitoring events, forecasting trends, and writing reports or articles. Current AI tools can already accelerate literature review, document analysis, data coding, drafting, and scenario generation, though humans remain important for research design, credibility, institutional knowledge, and judgment in politically sensitive contexts. Demand elasticity is limited because most employment is in government or grant-funded settings where budgets, headcount, and the number of major policy decisions do not expand proportionally when analysis becomes cheaper. With high disruption and relatively low demand expansion, AI is likely to reduce the need for some analysts while leaving a smaller set of senior experts and client-facing researchers.

title: Postal service workers
rationale: Postal service work is heavily physical and place-based: carriers walk or drive routes, handle parcels, collect signatures, and interact with real-world addresses and customers. AI and automation can materially improve sorting, address recognition, routing, customer-service kiosks, and back-office processing, but the largest share of the occupation still requires physical delivery and local presence. Demand elasticity is low because total letter-mail volume is structurally declining and households or businesses are unlikely to send dramatically more mail just because processing is cheaper, although parcels may see some limited expansion. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation fits the resilient category even though employment may continue to decline from automation and digital substitution.

title: Postsecondary education administrators
rationale: Much of this occupation consists of digital and language-heavy administrative work: application review, student communications, records management, scheduling, reporting, policy drafting, and data analysis are all directly affected by AI. Human judgment, campus presence, relationship management, crisis response, and institutional leadership remain important, but many registrar, admissions, and routine student-services workflows can be substantially automated or handled by AI-assisted systems. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of students, institutions, courses, and formal administrative decisions does not expand dramatically just because administration becomes cheaper. Given high disruption and limited demand expansion, AI is likely to reduce headcount in routine administrative roles while leaving a smaller set of higher-skill human administrators overseeing systems and handling complex cases.

title: Postsecondary teachers
rationale: Postsecondary teaching is heavily cognitive, language-based, and digital in many of its core tasks: preparing lectures, creating assignments, grading, advising, writing research papers, reviewing literature, and designing curricula are all directly affected by AI tools. However, the occupation is not fully automatable because universities sell credentials, mentorship, research supervision, lab or studio experiences, peer interaction, and institutional authority, all of which still require human faculty presence. Demand for higher education and lifelong learning could expand if instruction becomes cheaper and more personalized, but accreditation, public funding, degree requirements, campus capacity, and the prestige value of human faculty limit elasticity. The likely outcome is substantial restructuring: fewer purely lecture-and-grading roles, more AI-enabled course design, advising, research supervision, and high-touch mentorship roles.

title: Power plant operators, distributors, and dispatchers
rationale: The occupation is heavily centered on monitoring instruments, interpreting system data, adjusting controls, and issuing dispatch or switching instructions, all of which are increasingly exposed to automation, smart-grid systems, predictive maintenance, anomaly detection, and AI-assisted optimization.
